ARCHITECTO ROBERTO ADAM

Pages 140-150

Q. F. F. Q. S. The east and west fronts of this pile are to extend 255 feet, and the south and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> 358. There are to be houses for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> and six <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of the professors. The library is to be a room of 160 feet in length; the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities is to be of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and the dimensions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> for degrees and public exercises are about 90 feet by 30. There are likewise to be an elegant and most convenient anatomical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>; a chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LABORATORY">laboratory</a>; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> rooms for instruments and experiments for the professors of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. The whole, when finished, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the most splendid structure of the sort in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> however be the completest and most commodious. The progress of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> has now (1804) stopped. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> was completed by the aid of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> munificence; but after an expenditure of 50,000l. it is supposed that not more than one third of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> has been executed. The botanical garden belonging to the university is situated at the distance of about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> between <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEITH">Leith</a>. It consists of about five acres of ground; and is furnished with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, many of them brought from the most distant <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of the globe. The professor's botanist to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, and receives a salary of 120l. annually for the support of the garden. A monument, to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of the celebrated botanist Linnaeus, was erected here by the late Dr Hope, who first planned the garden, and Edinburgh brought it to perfection. The university of Edinburgh, like the others in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, sends one member to the General <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland; and the widows of the professors have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the funds of those of ministers, the professors being <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> on that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> along with the presbytery of Edinburgh. "In the year 1772, the Board of Trustees for the encouragement of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">Manufactures</a>, &c., in Scotland, appointed Mr Alexander Runciman, painter, to teach 23 boys or girls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>, allowing him a yearly salary of 120l. He was succeeded in this office by Mr Allan, to whom followed Mr Graham. This <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> being appropriated for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of manufactures, is not properly a school of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>. In this last art, however, very eminent teachers are to be found in Edinburgh, but no public establishment exists for its encouragement. "Near the University there is also a Riding School, called the Royal Academy for teaching Exercises. The teacher of this academy receives a salary of 200l. a-year from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and is accommodated with a riding school of 120 feet in length by 40 in breadth, and stables to a considerable extent. "In Edinburgh there is established, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of that in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, a Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, which has published some volumes of transactions. It contains a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of members of great respectability; but in Edinburgh men of letters are apt to be extremely jealous and unsociable with regard to each other. This illiberality of temper prevents the Royal Society from being of much value. Great numbers of the most accomplished and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> men of letters are unconnected with it, while it contains others who have been introduced to it merely by their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in the world, or the circumstance of having attained to distinguished literary situations by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of men in power, who of late years have, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, displayed little of that anxiety to discriminate and bring into notice men of literary talents, which once formed the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> characteristic of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> and gentlemen of Scotland." 13. The Royal Infirmary was first thought of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> of Physicians in 1725. A <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> happening to be dissolved at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, the partners contributed some of their stock towards the establishment of the Infirmary. A subscription was also let on foot, and application made to the General Assembly to recommend the same throughout their jurisdiction. This was readily complied with, and the assembly passed an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> for that purpose; but very little regard was paid to it by the clergy. Notwithstanding this, however, 200l. being procured, a small <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> was opened for the reception of the sick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> in August 1729. In 1736, the contributors towards the Infirmary were erected into a body corporate by royal statute; and after this the contributions increased very considerably: by which means the managers were enabled to enlarge their scheme from time to time; and at last to undertake the present magnificent structure, the foundation of which was laid in 1738. During 25 years, when this institution was in its infancy, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Hopetoun bestowed upon it an annuity of 200l. In 1750, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> Archibald Ker bequeathed to this incorporation 200l. a-year in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Jamaica. In 1755, the lords, Edinburgh: lords of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> made a donation to it of £8000, which had been appointed for the support of invalids. In return for this, the managers of the Infirmary constantly keep 60 beds in readiness for the reception of sick <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. This year also sick servants began to be admitted into the Infirmary, and a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a> was fitted up for their reception. This institution, however, was more indebted to George Drummond, Esq., than to any other person. He was seven times chosen lord provost of Edinburgh; and always directed his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the improvement of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, particularly to that of the Royal Infirmary. So sensible were the managers of their obligations to him, that, in their hall, they erected a bust of him with this inscription, "George Drummond, to whom this country is indebted for all the benefit which it derives from the Royal Infirmary." In 1748, the stock of the Infirmary amounted to £3000; in 1755, to £7000; besides the estate left by Doctor Ker; in 1764, to £23,426; and in 1778, to £27,074. The Royal Infirmary is attended by two physicians chosen by the managers, who visit their patients daily in presence of the students. All the members of the College of Surgeons were obliged to attend in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a>, according to seniority. If any surgeon declined attendance, he was not allowed to appoint a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>; and the patients were committed to the care of one of four assistant surgeons, chosen annually by the managers: this was formerly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of attendance, but the managers have in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a decision of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of judicature assumed to themselves the sole right of electing the surgeons.—From the year 1762 to 1769, there were admitted 6261 patients; which number added to 109 who were in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at the commencement of the year 1762, made, in all, 6370. Of these, 4395 were cured; 358 died; the rest were either relieved, dismissed incurable, for irregularities, or by their own desire, or remained in the hospital.—From 1770 to 1775, the patients annually admitted into the Infirmary were, at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, 1567; of whom 63 died. In 1776, there were admitted 1668, of whom 57 died; and in 1777, the number admitted was 1593, and of deaths, 52. In the year 1786, there were admitted 1822 patients: Of these 1354 were cured; 166 relieved; 84 died; the rest were either relieved, dismissed incurable, for irregularities, or by their own desire. The building consists of a body and two wings, each of them three stories high, with an attic story and garrets, and a very elegant front. The body is 210 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and 36 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> in the middle, but at the ends only 24 feet broad. There is a bust of King George II. in a Roman dress, above the great door. The wings are 70 feet long, and 25 broad. In the centre is a large staircase, so wide that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">sedan</a> chairs may be carried up. In the different wards, 228 patients may be accommodated, each in a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> for the patients, and also for the citizens; and to these last the patients are never admitted. Besides the apartments necessary for the sick, there are others for the officers and servants belonging to the house. There are likewise rooms for the managers, a consulting room for the physicians and surgeons—a waiting room for the students, and a theatre that will hold upwards of 200 people for performing surgical operations. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> ward, supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the £8000 already mentioned; and in consequence of which a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> is always kept at the Infirmary. The wards for sick servants are supported by collections at the church doors. Besides the surgical attendance already mentioned, there are two physicians belonging to the house, who are elected by the managers, and have a salary: there is likewise a house-surgeon and apothecary. Students who attend the Infirmary paid formerly 3l. 3s. which is increased to 5l. 5s. annually, which brings in a considerable revenue towards defraying the expense of the house. Two wards are set apart for the patients whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> are supposed to be most interesting; and the medical professors in the university give clinical lectures upon them by rotation. 14. The Public Dispensary was founded by Dr Duncan in 1776, for the poor whose diseases are of such a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> as to render their admission into the Infirmary either unnecessary or improper. Here the patients receive advice gratis four days in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> is kept of the diseases of each, and of the effects produced by the medicines employed. All patients not improper for dispensary treatment are admitted on the recommendation of the elder or church warden of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> where they reside. The physicians officiate and give lectures gratis; so that the apothecary who lodges in the house, and the medicines, are the only expenses attending this useful institution. The expense of the whole is defrayed by public contributions, and from a small annual fee paid by the students who attend the lectures. It is under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, two vice-presidents, and 20 directors, elected annually from among the contributors. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> entitles a contributor to recommend patients and be a governor for two years, and five guineas gives the same privilege for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Under the same management there is an institution for the gratuitous <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INOCULATION">inoculation</a> for the cowpox. 15. The High School. The earliest institution of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school in Edinburgh seems to have been about the year 1519. The whole expense bestowed upon the first building of this kind amounted only to about 40l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. Another building, which had been erected for the accommodation of the scholars in 1578, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, notwithstanding the great increase of their number, to be used for that purpose till 1777. The foundation of the present new building was laid on the 24th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> that year by Sir William Forbes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> of the Free Masons. The total length of this building is 120 feet from south to north; the breadth in the middle 36, at each end 38 feet. The great hall where the boys meet for prayers, is 68 feet by 30l. At each end of the hall is a room of 32 feet by 20, intended for <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a>. The building is two stories high, the one 18, the other 17, feet in height. The expense of the whole was reckoned at 4000l. There is a rector and four masters, who teach from 400 to 500 scholars annually. The salaries are trifling, and the fees depend upon the reputation they have obtained for teaching; and as this has been for some years very considerable, the rector's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is supposed to be worth not less than 400l. per annum, a master's about half that sum. There is a janitor, whose place is supposed to be worth about 70l. a-year. His business is to take care of the boys on the play ground; and there is a woman who lives on the spot as under-janitor, whose place may be worth about £21 annually. There is a library, but not large, as each of the boys pays only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> annually to its support. There are four established English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> in Edinburgh; the masters of which receive a small salary, upon express condition that they shall not take above a limited sum per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> from any of their scholars. There are likewise many other private schools in Edinburgh for all languages; and, in general, every kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> is to be had here in great perfection and at a very cheap rate. 16. The Mint is kept up by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of Union, with all the offices belonging to it, though no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is ever struck here. It stands in the Cowgate, a little to the west of the English church; but is in a ruined state, though still inhabited by the different officers, who have free houses; and the bellman enjoys his salary by regularly ringing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELL">bell</a>. This place, as well as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of Holyroodhouse, is an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for debtors. 17. The English Chapel stands near the Cowgate Port, and was founded on the 3d of April 1771. The foundation <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> was laid by General Oughton, with the following inscription: Edificii sacri Ecclesiae episc. Anglicae, primum posuit lapidem J. Adolphus Oughton, in archetectonice Scotiae repub. curio maximus, militum praefectus, regnante Georgio III. tertio Ap. die, A.D. MDCCCLXXI. It is a plain handsome building, neatly fitted up in the inside, and somewhat resembling the church of St Martin's in the Fields, London. It is 90 feet long, 75 broad, and ornamented with an elegant spire of considerable height. It is also furnished with an excellent bell, formerly belonging to the chapel royal at Holyroodhouse, which is permitted to be rung for assembling the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>; an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> not granted to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a> in England. The expense of the building was defrayed by voluntary subscription; and to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the country, people of all persuasions contributed to this pious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. It has already cost £7000, and will require £1000 more to finish the portico. This church is built in a singular manner, viz. from south to north, and the altar-piece stands on the east side. Three clergymen officiate here, of whom the first has £150, the other two £100 each: the altar-piece is finely decorated, and there is a good organ. There is another Episcopal chapel, but small, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACKFRIARS">Blackfriars</a> wynd, which was founded by Baron Smith in the year 1722. There are also some meetings of the Episcopal church of Scotland, who adhere to their old forms, having still their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> and inferior clergy. For some time these were subjected to penal laws, as they refused to take the oath to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, or mention the present royal family in their public prayers: but having conformed, and taken the oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, Edinburgh, their conduct has been approved of by his majesty; so that now every denomination of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> pray for the royal family on the throne. 18. Heriot's Hospital owes its foundation to George Heriot, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDSMITH">goldsmith</a> to James VI, who acquired by his business a large fortune. At his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he left the magistrates of Edinburgh £23,625.10s. "for the maintenance, relief, and bringing up of so many poor and fatherless boys, freemen's sons of the town of Edinburgh," as the above sum should be sufficient for. This hospital is finely situated on the west end of the fourth ridge, almost opposite to the castle, and is the most magnificent building of the kind in Edinburgh. It was founded in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1628, according to a plan (as is reported) of Inigo Jones; but the work being interrupted by the civil wars, it was not finished till the year 1650. The expense of the building is said to have been upwards of £30,000. (a) and the hospital is now possessed of an income of about £3000 a-year; though this cannot be absolutely ascertained, as the rents are paid in grain, and of course must be fluctuating. It stands on a rising ground to the south-west of the city, and is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> of 162 feet without, having a court 94 feet square in the inside, with piazzas on three of the sides. There is a spire with a clock over the gateway, and each corner of the building is ornamented with turrets; but notwithstanding the magnificent appearance of the outside, the inner <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> is far from being convenient. There is a statue of the founder over the gateway, in the dress of the times, and a very good painting of him in the governors' room, with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Mr Carmichael. There is a chapel 61 feet long and 22 broad, which is now repairing in such a manner as will make it worthy of notice. When Cromwell took possession of Edinburgh after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUNBAR">Dunbar</a>, he quartered his sick and wounded soldiers in this hospital. It was applied to the same purpose till the year 1658, when General Monk, at the request of the governors, removed the soldiers; and on the 11th of April 1659, it was opened for the reception of boys, 30 of whom were admitted into it. The August after, they were increased to 40; and in 1661, to 52. In 1753 the number was raised to 130, and in 1763 to 140; but since that time it has decreased.—In this hospital the boys are instructed in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, and a knowledge of the Latin tongue. With such as choose to follow any kind of trade, an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a> fee of £10 is given when they leave the hospital; and those who choose an academical education, have an annuity of £10 a-year bestowed on them for four years. The whole is under the oversight of the treasurer, who has under him a house governor, housekeeper, and schoolmasters. (a) It is to be observed, that money then bore 10l. per cent. interest.—The above sums are taken from Mr Arnott's <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Edinburgh, who subjoins the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. "Where Maitland had collected his most erroneous account of George Heriot's effects we do not know. He makes the sum received, out of Heriot's effects, by the governors of the hospital, to be £43,608l. 11s. 3d. being almost <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> of what they really get. This blunder has been the cause of many unjust murmurings against the magistrates of Edinburgh, and even the means of spiriting up lawsuits against them." 19. Watson's Hospital has its name from the founder George Watson, who was at first clerk to Sir William Dick provost of Edinburgh in 1676, then accountant of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Scotland; after that he became receiver of the city's impost on ale, treasurer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">Merchants</a>' Maiden Hospital, and to the society for propagating Christian knowledge. Dying a bachelor in 1723, he left £2,000l. for the maintenance and education of the children and grandchildren of decayed members of the merchant company of Edinburgh. The scheme, however, was not put in execution till the year 1738, when the sum originally left had accumulated to £20,000l. The present building was then erected, in which about 60 boys are maintained and educated. It is much less magnificent than Heriot's hospital, but the building is far from being despised. It stands to the southward of the city at a small distance from Heriot's hospital, and was erected at the expense of £5000l.: its present revenue is about £1700l. It is under the management of the master, assistants, and treasurer of the Merchant Company, four old bailies, the old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of guild, and the two ministers of the Old church. The boys are genteely clothed and liberally educated. Such as choose an university education are allowed £10l. per annum for five years: those who go to trades have £20l. allowed them for their apprentice fee, and at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 25 years, if they have behaved properly, and not contracted <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> without consent of the governors, they receive a bounty of £50l. The boys are under the immediate inspection of the treasurer, schoolmaster, and housekeeper. 20. The Merchants' Maiden Hospital was established by voluntary contribution about the end of the last century, for the maintenance of young girls, daughters of the merchants burgesses of Edinburgh. The governors were erected into a body corporate, by act of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, in 1707. The annual revenue amounts to £1350l. Seventy girls are maintained in it; who, upon leaving the house, receive £1l. 6s. 8d. excepting a few who are allowed £8l. 6s. 8d. out of the funds of the hospital. The profits arising from work done in the house are also divided among the girls, according to their industry. 21. The Trades' Maiden Hospital was founded in the year 1704 by the incorporations of Edinburgh, for the maintenance of the daughters of decayed members, on a plan similar to that of the merchants hospital. To this, as well as to the former, one Mrs <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> Erskine, a widow, gentlewoman, contributed so liberally, that she was by the governors styled <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> founders of the hospital. Fifty girls are maintained in the house, who pay of entry money £1l. 13s. 4d.; and, when they leave it, receive a bounty of £1l. 11s. 4d. The revenues are estimated at £600l. a-year. 22. The Orphan Hospital was planned in 1732, by Andrew Gairdner merchant, and other inhabitants. It was promoted by the society for propagating Christian knowledge, by other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>, by voluntary subscriptions, and a collection at the church doors.—In 1733, the managers hired a house, took in 30 orphans, maintained them, gave them instructions in reading and writing, and taught them the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a> business. In 1735, they were erected into a body corporate by the town of Edinburgh: and, in 1742, they obtained a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of erection from his late majesty, appointing most of the great officers of state in Scotland, Edinburgh, and the heads of the different societies in Edinburgh, members of this corporation; with powers to them to hold real <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to the amount of £1000l. a-year. The revenue is inconsiderable; but the institution is supported by the contributions of charitable persons. Into this hospital orphans are received from any part of the kingdom. None are admitted under seven, nor continued in it after 14 years of age. The orphan hospital is situated to the east of the North <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>; and is a handsome building, consisting of a body and two wings, with a neat spire, furnished with a clock and two bells. The late worthy Mr Howard admits, that this institution is one of the most useful charities in Europe, and is a pattern for all institutions of the kind. The funds have been considerably increased, and the building greatly improved, through the attention and exertions of Mr Thomas Tod formerly treasurer. 23. The Trinity Hospital. This was originally founded and amply endowed by King James II.'s <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>. At the Reformation, it was stripped of its revenues; but the regent afterwards bestowed them on the provost of Edinburgh, who gave them to the citizens for the use of the poor. In 1585, the town <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> purchased from Robert Pont, at that time provost of Trinity college, his interest in these subjects; and the transaction was afterwards ratified by James VI. The hospital was then repaired, and appointed for the reception of poor old burgesses, their wives and unmarried children, not under 50 years of age. In the year 1700, this hospital maintained 54 persons; but, since that time, the number has decreased.—The revenue consists in a real estate of lands and houses, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> rents of which are £62l. a year, and £550l. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> out at bonds at 4 per cent. This hospital is situated at the foot of Leith wynd, and maintains about 50 of both sexes, who are comfortably lodged, each having a room for themselves. They are supplied with roast or boiled meat every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> for dinner, have money allowed them for clothes, and likewise a small sum for pocket money. There is a small library for their amusement, and they have a chaplain to say prayers. There are some out-pensioners who have £1l. a-year, but these are discouraged by the governors. The funds are under the management of the town council. 24. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">Charity</a> Workhouse was erected in 1743 by voluntary contribution. It is a large plain building, on the south side of the city. Here the poor are employed, and are allowed twopence out of every shilling they earn. The expense of this institution is supposed not to be less than £4000l. annually; as about 700 persons of both sexes, including children, are maintained here, each of whom cannot be reckoned to cost less than £1l. 10s. per annum; and there are besides 300 out-pensioners. The only permanent fund for defraying this expense is a tax of two per cent. on the valued rents of the city, which may bring in about £600l. annually; and there are other funds which yield about £400l. The rest is derived from collections at the church doors and voluntary contributions; but as these always <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> short of what is requisite, recourse must frequently be had to extraordinary collections. The sum arising from the rents of the city, however, is constantly... To the fourth-west of the castle, near a suburb called the Wright's House, on the site of a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> building, which was demolished to make way for it, Gillespie's Hospital has lately been erected. Its appellation is derived from the founder, an eminent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANUFACTURER">manufacturer</a> of snuff in Edinburgh. It is intended for the support of aged persons; and those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the name of the founder are preferred. It is a neat stone building, executed in a style of moderate expense, with a small tower in the centre and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and Gothic turrets at suitable distances around the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. Besides these there are to be found in Edinburgh several charitable establishments, which, though not furnished with costly buildings, are not of a less benevolent or valuable nature. Of these, one of the most distinguished is the Hospital or Workhouse, or Asylum, as it is called, for the Industrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLIND">Blind</a>; which is supported by the contributions of charitable persons, and by the price of the articles manufactured in it. Here the blind are taught such trades as may enable them to earn a subsistence, or at least aid them in contributing to their own support. They manufacture baskets, mats, &c.; and some of them have been taught to act as weavers, for which purpose they use the shuttle. The Magdalene Asylum also deserves notice; in which a most laudable attempt has of late years been made, by a benevolent society, to reclaim, from vice and misery, women who have degraded themselves by public prostitution, but who think fit to retire thither with the view of abandoning their mode of life, and of supporting themselves by industry. This institution is managed with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of care and delicacy which does the highest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to its patrons. The objects of this charity are kept concealed: they reap the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their own labour; and every effort is made to procure employment for them. In particular, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>-work of all sorts is executed in it in the neatest manner; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> is washed, at moderate prices, for such persons in the city as think fit to transmit these articles to the society. Besides all these charities, there is an hospital in the city for Lying-in Women, under the care of the professor of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MIDWIFERY">midwifery</a>: which is an institution analogous to that of the Royal Infirmary.—There is a Society for the Relief of the Destitute Sick, which has received considerable public countenance, though it has no appropriate building or local establishment.—An institution of a peculiar nature, not unconnected with the present subject, called the Repository, ought not to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unnoticed. It is a shop or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">ware</a>-room on South Bridge Street, to which ladies in straitened circumstances have an opportunity of sending for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> curious, beautiful, or useful articles of needle-work, with the price affixed. When a purchaser has been found for the goods, the proceeds are transmitted in such a manner as to prevent its being known to the public by whom the articles were prepared. This institution has been promoted by the Duchess of Buccleugh and many other persons of rank. There are two other charity workhouses in the suburbs, much on the same plan with that now described: one in the Canongate, and the other in St Cuthbert's Edinburgh, or West Kirk parish. To this account of the charitable establishments in Edinburgh, we shall add that of some others; which, though not calculated to decorate the city by any public building, are perhaps no less deserving of praise than any we have mentioned. The first is that of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> William <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>; who left £300l. in trust to the magistrates, the annual profits to be divided on Christmas day to poor out-door labourers, who must at that season of the year be destitute of employment; five pounds to be given to those who have large families, and one half to those who have smaller. Another charity is that of Robert Johnston, LL.D., of London, who in 1640 left £300l. to the poor of this city; £100l. to be employed in setting them to work, another £100l. to clothe the boys in Heriot's Hospital, and the third £100l. to bursars at the university. About the beginning of this century John Strachan left his estate of Craigcrook, now upwards of £300l. a-year, in trust to the presbytery of Edinburgh, to be by them disposed of in small annual sums to poor old people not under 65 years of age, and to orphans not above 12. There is besides a society for the support of the industrious poor, another for the indigent sick, and there are also many charity schools. Having thus given an account of the most remarkable edifices belonging to Old Edinburgh, we shall now proceed to those of the New Town. This is terminated on the east side by the Calton hill, round which there is a pleasant walk, and which affords one of the finest prospects that can be imagined, varying remarkably almost at every step. On this hill is a burying ground, which contains a fine monument to the memory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Hume the historian.—On the top is an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, the scheme for building which was first adopted in the year 1736; but the disturbance occasioned by the Porteous mob prevented anything from being done towards the execution of it at that time. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Morton afterwards gave £100l. for the purpose of building an observatory, and appointed Mr MacLaurin professor of mathematics, together with the principal and some professors of the university, trustees for managing the sum. Mr MacLaurin added to the money above mentioned the profits arising from a course of lectures which he read on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental philosophy</a>; which, with some other small sums, amounted in all to £300l.; but Mr MacLaurin dying, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> was dropped.—Afterwards the money was put into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of two persons who became <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKRUPT">bankrupt</a>; but a considerable dividend being obtained out of their effects, the principal and interest, about the year 1776, amounted to £400l. A plan of the building was made out by Mr Craig <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>; and the foundation stone was laid by Mr Stoddart, lord provost of Edinburgh, on the 23rd of August 1776. About this time, however, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> architect happening to come to Edinburgh, conceived the idea of giving the whole the appearance of a fortification, for which its situation on the top of the Calton hill was very much adapted. Accordingly a line was marked out for enclosing the limits of the observatory with a wall constructed... for pit and boxes; and 1s. 6d. for the gallery) 40l. or Edinburgh- 45l. a night. About this time an act of parliament was passed, prohibiting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of plays, except in a house licensed by the king. Of this the presby- tery of Edinburgh immediately laid hold; and at their own expense brought an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> on the statute against the players. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> was by the court of session decided against the players; who thereupon applied to parliament for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> to enable his majesty to license a theatre in Edinburgh. Against this bill petitions were presented in 1739 to the house of commons by the magistrates and town council, the principal and pro- fessors of the university, and the dean of guild and his council; in consequence of which, the affair was drop- ped. All this opposition, however, contributed in reality to the success of the players; for the spirit of party being excited, a way of evading the act was ea- ily found out, and the house was frequented more than usual, inasmuch that Taylor's Hall was found in- sufficient to contain the number of spectators. The comedians now fell out among themselves, and a new <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a> was erected in the Canongate in the year 1746. The consequence of this was, that the old one in Taylor's Hall became entirely deserted, and through bad conduct the managers of the new theatre soon found themselves greatly involved. At last, a riot ensuing through dissensions among the performers, the playhouse was totally demolished.—When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the royalty over the spot where the New Town is built was obtained, a clause was likewise added to the bill, enabling his majesty to license a theatre in Edin- burgh. This was obtained, and thus the opposition of the clergy for ever silenced. But notwithstanding this, the high price paid by the managers to the pa- tentee, being no less than 500 guineas annually, pre- vented them effectually from decorating the house as they would otherwise have done, or even from always retaining good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; by which means the success of the Edinburgh theatre has not been so great as might have been expected. Not far from this building, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a> was opened in 1792, on the road to Leith, for equestrian exhibitions, pantomime entertainments, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and tumbling. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> was 60 feet diameter; and in the forenoon ladies and gentlemen were taught to ride. The house held about 1500 people. This building has since converted into an elegant and commodious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> room. 27. The Register Office. This work was first fug- getted by the late Earl of Morton, lord-register of Scot- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, with a view to prevent the danger which attended the usual method of keeping the public records. In former times, indeed, these suffered from a variety of accidents. Edward I. carried off or destroyed most of them, in order to prevent any marks of the former in- dependence of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> from remaining to posterity. Afterwards Cromwell spoiled this nation of its records, most of which were sent to the Tower of London. At the time of the restoration, many of them were sent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> again by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; but one of the vessels was ship- wrecked, and the records brought by the other have ever since been left in the greatest confusion.—The Earl of Morton taking this into consideration, obtain- ed from his majesty a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of 12,000l. out of the for- feited estates, for the purpose of building a register office, Edinburgh office, or house for keeping the records, and disposing them in proper order. The foundation was laid on the 27th of June 1774, by Lord Frederic Campbell lord-register, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a> of Stainhowe lord advocate, and Mr Miller of Bariskinning lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> clerk; three of the trustees appointed by his majesty for executing the work. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> was performed under a discharge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, in presence of the judges of the courts of session and exchequer, and in the sight of a multitude of spectators. A <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> plate was put into the foundation stone with the following inscription: Conservandis Tabulis Publicis positum est, anno M.DCC.LXXIV, munificentia optimi et pietissimi principis Georgii Tertii. In a glass vase hermetically sealed, which is also placed in the foundation stone, are deposited specimens of the different coins of his present majesty. The front of the building directly faces the bridge, extends from east to west 100 feet, and is 40 feet back from the line of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>'s street. In the middle of the front is a small projection of three windows in breadth. Here is a pediment, having in its centre the arms of Great Britain, and the whole is supported by four Corinthian pilasters. At each end is a tower projecting beyond the rest of the building, having a Venetian window in front, and a cupola on the top. The front is ornamented from end to end with a beautiful Corinthian entablature. In the centre of the building is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOME">dome</a> of wooden work covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>. The inside forms a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALOON">saloon</a> 50 feet diameter and 80 high, lighted at top by a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> window 15 feet in diameter. Round the whole is a hanging gallery of stone, with an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> balustrade, which affords conveniency for preludes in the walls for keeping the records. The whole number of apartments is 97; all of which are vaulted beneath, and warmed with fire-places. This building, which is the most beautiful of Mr Adam's designs, has been executed in a substantial manner, in about 16 years, at the expense of near 40,000l. and is one of the principal ornaments of the city. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERGEANT">sergeant</a>'s guard is placed here from the castle, for the further protection of the records. It is intended to place a statue of his present majesty in the front of the building, with the lion and unicorn above the sentinels' boxes. The lord-registrar has the direction of the whole, and the principal clerks of session are his deputies. There have a great number of clerks under them for carrying on the business of the court of session. The lord-registrar is a minister of state in this country. He formerly collected the votes of the parliament of Scotland, and still collects those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of 16 to represent them in parliament. 27. On the east side of St. Andrew's square stands the General <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">Excise</a> Office, built by the late Sir Lawrence Dundas for his own residence, but sold by his son for the above purpose. It is a very handsome building, with a pediment in front ornamented with the king's arms, and supported by four Corinthian pilasters; and, in conjunction with the two corner houses, has a fine effect. 28. St. Andrew's Church stands on the north side of George's street. It is of an oval form; and has a very neat spire of 186 feet in height, with a chime of eight bells, the first and only one of the kind in Scotland. It has also a handsome portico in front. 29. Opposite to St. Andrew's church is the Physic Hall, designed for the meetings of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, and which has a portico resembling that of the church. 30. Farther to the westward, on the south side, stand the Assembly Rooms, which though a heavy looking building on the outside, are nevertheless extremely elegant and commodious within. The largest is 100 feet long and 40 broad, being exceeded in its dimensions by none in the island, the large one at Bath excepted. Weekly assemblies are held here for dancing and card-playing, under the direction of a master of ceremonies; admission tickets five shillings each. "There are three <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANKING">Banking</a> Companies in Edinburgh established by statute, or by royal charters. These are, the Bank of Scotland, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the Old Bank, the Royal Bank of Scotland, and the British Linen Company. 31. "The Bank of Scotland, commonly called the Old Bank, was erected by act of parliament, A.D. 1695. By the statute of erection, the company was empowered to raise a joint stock of 1,200,000l. Scots, or 100,000l. Sterling, for the purpose of carrying on a public bank. The smallest share which any person could hold in the bank was declared to be 100l. Scots; and the largest sum for which any one was allowed to subscribe was 20,000l. of the same money. Eight thousand are declared to be the qualification necessary to entitle any one to be elected governor; 600l. deputy governor; and 300l. for each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>. The management of the affairs of the company was vested in a governor, deputy governor, and twenty-four directors; and in choosing these managers, each proprietor was declared to have a vote for every 100l. of stock held by him. "The office of this company has hitherto been held in a house down a narrow lane at the south side of that part of the High street called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">Lawn</a>-market; but, at a great expense, they have erected for their accommodation a building which will speedily be ready to be occupied, and which is situated to the northward of the High street, in full view of Prince's street. This is at once a magnificent and beautiful fabric. The back of the building is towards Prince's street; and here, while erecting, it had the disadvantage, from its vast height, of having somewhat the aspect of a tower. This effect, however, is now removed by raising the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> for the purpose of covering up the lower part of it, and by a wall of considerable height in the nature of a curtain, which has been added to augment its apparent breadth. It forms, upon the whole, a beautiful and most superb fabric. As a work of magnitude, it is seen to most advantage from the mound of earth which connects the Old and the New Town, at that part of the mound which is in the direction of the north-west <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of the building. Here the eye is filled by the full view of two sides of the fabric, and by a display of its great height. The result of which is, that as a magnificent and stupendous structure, it seems to have no rival in this country. "This banking company has established branches in every considerable town in Scotland, excepting Glasgow, which, in consequence of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> adjustment to avoid rivalryship, is left to the Royal Bank. By agreement, the latter has a branch at Glasgow, and no branch in any other town in Scotland." 33. "The Royal Bank was established in the following manner: By the articles of union, Scotland was declared to be liable to the same duties which were levied by way of customs or excise in England. As these duties had, in the latter of these nations, been appropriated for the discharge of debts contracted by England before the union, it was found reasonable to give Scotland an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> for this additional burden. The sum, given by way of equivalent, was ordained to be paid for certain purposes, and to certain persons or bodies corporate, mentioned in the articles of union and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> statutes. The proprietors of these sums, to the extent of £248,550 sterling, were erected into a body corporate, under the name of the Equivalent Company; and the said sum of £248,550, was declared to be the joint stock of the company. Upon application by this company, they obtained a royal charter, empowering such of them as inclined to subscribe their shares in the joint stock for that purpose, to carry on the business of banking. By this charter the subscribers to this banking business were, in A.D. 1727, erected into a body corporate, to be called, "The Royal Bank of Scotland." They were vested with the requisite powers, and the management of the company's affairs declared to be in a governor, deputy governor, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> ordinary and nine extraordinary directors. The qualifications of these managers were declared to be, that of the governor to hold stock to the extent of £2000; of the deputy governor, of £1500; of the ordinary directors, of £1000; and of the extraordinary directors, of £500. The sum originally subscribed was £111,000; but by a charter passed in favour of the Royal Bank, A.D. 1738, explaining the privileges formerly bestowed upon them, and enabling them to increase their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, they were empowered to raise their stock to a sum not exceeding in whole, when joined to their original funds, £150,000. By the charter of erection of this company, a share of £300 entitles a proprietor to one vote, one of £500, to two, of £1000, to three, and of £2000, to four; and no proprietor can have more than four votes. 34. "The British Linen Company, with a capital of £100,000, was incorporated by royal charter in 1746, with a view to encourage the manufacture of linen in Scotland. By the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of this company, its affairs are declared to be under the management of a governor, deputy governor, and five directors. It is declared a necessary qualification in the governor to be possessed of a share in the company's stock to the amount of £1000; of the deputy governor, £500; and of each director, of £300. A share of £200 entitles a proprietor to vote in the choice of these managers, of £500, to two votes, and of £1000, to four votes; but it is declared that no proprietor shall possess more than four votes. "This company carries on the business of banking, and issues promissory notes like the two former companies; but the banking business is carried on separately from the linen trade. The Linen Hall remains in the Canongate; but the apartments of the bank are removed to a lane on the south side of the High street, above what was called the Nether-bow port. "Promissory notes, payable on demand, have also been long issued in Edinburgh by a private banking house, that of Sir William Forbes, Sir James Hunter, and Company; and their notes have possessed a most extensive circulation. "Besides these there are several private banking houses of great reputation in Edinburgh, which do not issue promissory notes for small sums payable on demand, but which carry on the other branches of the banking trade, by transmitting money, discounting bills, and accommodating individuals with cash accounts." It now remains only to speak something of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and civil establishments of this <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. The highest of the former is the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland, who meet here annually in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May, in an aisle of the church of St Giles fitted up on purpose for them. The throne is filled by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> from his majesty, but he neither debates nor votes. He calls them together, and dissolves them at the appointed time in the name of the king; but they call and dissolve themselves in the name of the Lord <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ. This assembly consists of 350 members chosen out of the various presbyteries throughout the kingdom; and the debates are often very interesting and eloquent. This is the supreme <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> court in Scotland, to which appeals <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> from the inferior ones. The ecclesiastical court next in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> to the assembly is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">Synod</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TWEEDDALE">Tweeddale</a>, who meet in the same place in April and November; and next to them is the Presbytery of Edinburgh. These meet on the last Wednesday of every month, and are trustees on the fund for ministers widows. They have a hall in Scott's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, where there is a good picture of Dr Webster by Martin, which was put up at the expense of the trustees, out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the trouble he took in planning and fully establishing the fund. The Society for propagating Christian Knowledge in the Highlands and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a> of Scotland, was established a body corporate by Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> in the year 1709, for the purpose of erecting schools to instruct poor children in the principles of Christianity, as well as in reading and writing. The society have a hall in Warriston's close where their business is transacted. From time to time they have received large contributions, which have always been very properly applied; and for much the same purpose his majesty gives £1000 annually to the general assembly of the church of Scotland, which is employed by a committee of their number for instructing the poor Highlanders in the principles of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. The Erse church at Edinburgh was built about 30 years ago by subscriptions for the same laudable purpose. Great numbers of people <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to the metropolis from the Highlands, who understand no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> but their own, and consequently have no opportunity of instruction without it; and a most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the benefit they have received from it is, that though the church is capable of holding 1000 people, yet it is not large enough for those who apply for seats. The minister has £100 per annum arising from the seat rents, and holds <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the church of Scotland. The establishment was promoted by William Dickson dyer in Edinburgh. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> constitution of Edinburgh, the town council have the direction of all public affairs. The ordinary council consists only of 25 persons; but the council ordinary and extraordinary, of 33. The whole is composed of merchants and tradesmen, whose respective powers and interests are so interwoven, that a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> is preserved between the two bodies. The members of the town council are partly elected by the members of the 14 incorporations, and they partly choose their own successors. The election is made in the following manner: First, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> or list of six persons is made out by each incorporation; from which number, the deacon belonging to the incorporation must be chosen. These lists are then laid before the ordinary council of 25, who "shorten the lists," by expunging one half of the names from each; and from the three remaining ones the deacon is to be chosen. When this election is over, the new deacons are presented to the ordinary council, who choose six of them to be members of their body, and the six deacons of last year then walk off. The council of 25 next proceed to the election of three merchant and two trades councillors. The members of council, who now amount to 33 in number, then make out lists, from which the lord provost, dean of guild, treasurer, and bailies, must be chosen. The candidates for each of these offices are three in number; and the election is made by the 30 members of council already mentioned, joined to the eight extraordinary council deacons. The lord provost of Edinburgh, who is styled right honourable, is high <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, coroner, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>, within the city and liberties, and the town, harbour, and road of Leith. He has also a jurisdiction in matters of life and death. He is preses of the convention of royal boroughs, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a> of the trained bands, commander of the city guard and of Edinburgh jail. In the city he has the precedence of all the great officers of state and of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; walking on the right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the king or of his majesty's commissioner; and has the privilege of having a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> and mace carried before him. Under him are four magistrates called bailies, whose office is much the same with that of aldermen in London. There is also a dean of guild, who has the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the public buildings, and without whose warrant no house nor building can be erected within the city. He has a council to consult with, a nominal treasurer, who formerly had the keeping of the town's money, which is now given to the chamberlain. These seven are elected annually; who with the seven of the former year, three merchants and two trades councillors, and 14 deacons or preses of incorporated trades, making in all 33, form the council of the city, and have the sole management and disposal of the city revenues; by which means they have the disposal of places to the amount of 20,000l. annually. Formerly the provost was also an officer in the Scots parliament. The magistrates are sheriffs-depute and justices of the peace; and the town council are also patrons for all the churches in Edinburgh, patrons of the university, and electors of the city's representative in parliament. They have besides a very ample jurisdiction both civil and criminal. They are superiors of the Canongate, Portsburgh, and Leith; and appoint over these certain of their own number, who are called baron bailies: but the person who presides over Leith has the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of admiral because he hath there a jurisdiction over <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs. The baron bailies appoint one or two of the inhabitants of their respective districts to be their substitutes, and these are called resident bailies. They hold courts in absence of the baron bailies, for petty offences and diffusing civil causes of little moment. No city in the world affords greater security to the inhabitants in their persons and properties than Edinburgh. Robberies are here very rare, and street <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> hardly known in the memory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; so that a person may walk the streets at any <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of the night in perfect security. This is in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> owing to the town guard. This institution originated from the consternation into which the citizens were thrown after the guard battle at Flowden. At that time, the town council commanded the inhabitants to assemble in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the city, and every fourth man to be on duty each night. This introduced a kind of personal duty for the defence of the town, called watching and warding; by which the trading part of the inhabitants were obliged in person to watch alternately, in order to prevent or suppress occasional disturbances. This, however, becoming in time extremely inconvenient, the town council, in 1648, appointed a body of 60 men to be raised; the captain of which was to have a monthly pay of 11l. 2s. 3d., two lieutenants of 2l. each, two sergeants of 1l. 5s. and the private men of 15s. each. No regular fund was established for defraying this expense: the consequence of which was, that the old method of watching and warding was resumed, but the people on whom this service devolved were now become so relaxed in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, that the magistrates were threatened with having the king's troops quartered in the city if they did not appoint a sufficient guard. On this 40 men were raised in 1679, and in 1682 the number was increased to 158. After the Revolution, the town council complained of the guard as a grievance, and requested parliament that it might be removed. Their request was immediately granted, and the old method of watching and warding was renewed. This, however, was now so intolerable, that the very next year they applied to parliament for leave to raise 126 men for the defence of the city, and to tax the citizens for their payment. This being granted, the corps was raised which still continues under the name of the town guard. At present the establishment consists of three officers and about 90 men, who mount guard by turns. The officers have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>'s pay; the sergeants, corporals, drummers, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> soldiers, the same with those of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. Their arms are the same with those of the king's forces; but when called upon to quell mobs, they use Lochaber axes, a part of the ancient Scottish armour now in use only among themselves. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a> or trained band of the city consist of 16 companies of 100 men each. They were in use to trained turn out every king's birthday; but only the officers' bands now remain, who are chosen annually. They consist of 16 captains and as many lieutenants and ensigns; the provost, as has already been mentioned, being the colonel. The town guard are paid chiefly by a tax on the trading people; these being the only persons formerly subject to watching and warding. This tax, how- Edinburgh, ever, amounts only to £1250l., and as the expense of the guard amounts to £1400l., the magistrates are obliged to defray the additional charge by other means. But in the year 1805, in consequence of a new system of <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a> being established, the city guard was reduced to one lieutenant, two sergeants, two corporals, two drummers, and thirty men, the lord provost for the time being to be captain, without pay, and the company to be armed and clothed at the expense of the city, but their pay to be defrayed out of the general fund raised under the new police act; and the duty of this company is to attend upon his majesty's commissioner to the general assembly of the church of Scotland, the magistrates and town council, the supreme courts of justice, and to act in general for the support of the new system of police. The system of police above alluded to, was established in 1805 by act of parliament, under the authority of which the city and suburbs are divided into six districts or wards for the more convenient execution of the purposes to which the act extends. The regulations included under this system of police relate to cleaning and lighting the streets and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in the city and suburbs, apprehending and punishing vagrants and disorderly persons, suppressing common begging, preventing nuisances and obstructions, and for other purposes connected with the preservation of peace and good order. The management of the whole affairs under this system of police is entrusted to the general and resident commissioners. The general commissioners appointed by the act, are, the lord provost and magistrates of the city of Edinburgh, with the lord president of the court of session, the lord justice clerk, the lord <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> baron of the court of exchequer, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> officers of the crown, and several other public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, in conjunction with the whole resident commissioners in the different wards. There are to be seven resident commissioners in each ward, the two highest in the list to go out, and two others to be elected in their stead annually; the commissioners to be occupiers of houses valued at twenty pounds sterling of free rent yearly, excepting in two wards, where occupying a house of twelve pounds rent is a sufficient qualification. In each ward there are to be elected by the resident commissioners, with the approbation of the general commissioners, an inspector, and such a number of officers of police and watchmen as may be necessary, the officers of police and watchmen upon duty having the authority and possessing the powers given by the law of Scotland to the office of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTABLE">constable</a>. The general commissioners have the power of choosing a superintendent or master of police for the whole city and suburbs included in the act, and to appoint a clerk who shall do the duty of clerk to the general meetings, as well as to the court of police to be held by the superintendent. The general commissioners also are authorized to fix the number of officers and watchmen to be employed in the different wards. The superintendent of police having been appointed by the commissioners, is to receive from the sheriff depute of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Edinburgh the authority of a sheriff substitute, as well as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of sheriff depute within the city and liberties from the lord provost who is principal sheriff within these bounds, that the superintendent acting as master or judge of police may have the full powers of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> in the execution of his duty. By the powers with which the superintendent is invested, he may commit offenders to the tolbooth or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDEWELL">bridewell</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> not exceeding 60 days, and impose fines for offences not exceeding 40 shillings sterling, and give judgment in damages for any sum not exceeding three pounds sterling with the expenses in either case. From the sentences of the superintendent there is no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the sheriff depute of the county, or to the lord provost as sheriff principal within the city. The superintendent of police is also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLET">billet</a>-master within his bounds, and the inspectors of wards are billet-masters within their several wards. The inspectors also have the powers of procurator fiscaux with respect to all prosecutions for offences committed within their bounds. The expenses necessary to carry the above act into execution, are to be defrayed from a fund raised by assessment on the inhabitants of three per cent. on the free rent of houses, shops or warehouses, and for the expenses of clothing and alimenting the persons committed to bridewell a farther assessment not exceeding ½ per cent. of the free rent of such houses, &c. For the purpose of ascertaining rents, surveyors are appointed; and if the rent fixed by them should be over-rated, an appeal may be made to a committee of the general commissioners specially appointed. The office of the superintendent of police is in the Lawnmarket. The operation of the act has only continued for a few months (September 1805) and although some complaints have been made of its rigorous execution, arising probably from such unavoidable and unforeseen circumstances as frequently occur in the establishment of a new system, yet there is every reason to hope, that it will prove highly beneficial for the preservation of peace and good order in the city and suburbs over which it extends. The number of inhabitants in the city of Edinburgh is somewhat uncertain, and has been very variously calculated. By a survey made in the year 1775, it appears that the number of families in the city, Canongate, and other suburbs, and the town of Leith, amounted to 13,806. The difficulty therefore is to fix the number of persons in a family. Dr Price fixes this number at 4½; Mr Maitland, at 5½; and Mr Arnot, at 6½; so that, according to this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>, the whole number of inhabitants is 82,836; to which he thinks 1,400 more may be added for those in the garrison, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, &c. The following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> exhibits a comparative view of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the city of Edinburgh and suburbs taken in different years. The last enumeration made in 1801 by act of parliament is supposed to be considerably defective in the real amount of the inhabitants, as an alarm was industriously spread that it was done with a view to the imposition of new taxes. This, it appeared, induced many to conceal the names and number of the individuals in their families, | Year | Population | |------|------------| | 1678 | 35,500 | | 1722 | 40,420 | | 1755 | 57,195 | | 1775 | 70,430 | | 1791 | 84,886 | | 1801 | 82,560 | There There are in Edinburgh 14 incorporations, capable of choosing their own deacons, viz. The royal college of surgeons; the corporations of goldsmiths, skinners, furriers, hammermen, wrights and masons, tailors, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAKERS">bakers</a>, butchers, shoemakers, weavers, waukers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONNET">bonnet</a>-makers, and merchant company. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> of Edinburgh are plentifully supplied with all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Fresh <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> meat, as well as fowl and fish, if the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> permit, may be had every day; and no city can be better supplied with garden stuffs. The Edinburgh strawberries particularly are remarkably large and fine. A striking instance of the plenty of provisions with which Edinburgh is supplied was observed in the year 1779, when several large fleets, all of them in want of necessaries, arrived in the Forth, to the amount of about 500 sail, and having on board at least 20,000 men; yet the increased consumption of provisions, which certainly ensued upon the arrival of so many strangers, made not the least increase in the rate of the markets, insomuch that several victualling ships sent down by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> board returned without opening their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HATCHES">hatches</a>. The city <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a> are let to the corporation of bakers in Edinburgh; and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> made in the city is remarkable for its goodness. Edinburgh is supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> brought for some miles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, and lodged in two reservoirs, from whence it is distributed through the city both to public <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> and private families. A revenue accrues to the town from the latter, which must undoubtedly increase in proportion as the city extends in magnitude. There are but few merchants in Edinburgh, most of them residing at the port of Leith; so that the support of the city depends on the consumption of the necessaries as well as the superfluities of life. There are five different sorts of people on whom the shopkeepers, publicans, and different trades depend: 1. The people of the law, who are a very respectable body in the city. 2. The number of young people of both sexes who come to town for their education, many of the parents of whom come along with them. 3. The country gentlemen, gentlemen of the army and navy, and people who have made their fortunes abroad, &c., all of whom come to attend the public diversions, or to spend their time in such a manner as is most agreeable to them. 4. The vast concourse of travellers from all parts. 5. Most of the money drawn for the rents of country gentlemen is circulated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a> or other agents. At Edinburgh there are excellent manufactures of linen and cambrics; there are also manufactures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in the neighbourhood, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> is carried on very extensively.
