As they went northward along the island, they found the ground still of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; till at last they met with a rock of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> black melted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, which seemed to contain some <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and on which was neither <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> nor grass, nor any mark of vegetation. Notwithstanding this general barrenness, however, there are several large tracts covered with cultivated soil, which produces potatoes of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour as sweet as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARROTS">carrots</a>, plantains, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> canes. The soil is a dry hard clay: and the inhabitants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the grass which grows between the stones in other parts of the island as a manure, and for preserving their vegetables when young from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The most remarkable curiosity belonging to this island is a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of colossal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>; of which, however, very few remain entire. These statues are placed only on the sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. On the east side of the island were seen the ruins of three platforms of stone <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, on each of which stood four of these large statues; but they were all fallen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from two of them, and one from the third: they were broken or defaced by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> measured one that had fallen, which was 15 feet in length, and six <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> over the shoulders: each statue had on its head a large cylindrical stone of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> colour, wrought perfectly round. Others were found that measured near 27 feet, and upwards of eight feet over the shoulders; and a still larger one was seen standing, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of which was sufficient to shelter all the party, consisting of near 30 persons, from the rays of the sun. The workmanship is rude, but not bad, nor are the features of the face ill formed; the ears are long, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTORTION">distortion</a> practised in the country, and the bodies have hardly any thing of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> figure about them. How these islanders, wholly unacquainted with any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> power, could raise such stupendous figures, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the large cylindric stones upon their heads, is truly wonderful! The most probable conjecture seems to be, that the stone is fictitious; and that each figure was gradually erected, by forming a temporary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> round it, and raising it as the work advanced; but they are at any rate very strong proofs of the ingenuity and perseverance of the islanders in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> when they were built, as well as that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of the present <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> had been better days than their descendants enjoy. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of this island is in general brackish, there being only one well that is perfectly fresh, which is at the east end of the island; and whenever the natives repair to it to flake their thirst, they wash themselves all over; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there is a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, the first leaps into the middle of the hole, drinks, and washes himself without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; after which another takes his place, and so on in succession. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> was much disdained by their new friends, who stood greatly in need of this valuable article, and did not wish to have it contaminated by such ablutions. The people are of a middle size. In general they are rather thin; go entirely naked; and have punctures on their bodies, a custom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to all the inhabitants of the South Sea <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Their greatest singularity is the size of their ears, the lobe of which is stretched out so that it almost rests on their shoulder; and is pierced with a very large hole, capable of admitting four or five fingers with ease. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> ornaments for their ears are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> down of feathers, and rings which they wear in the inside of the hole, made of the sugar <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, which is very <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, and for this purpose is rolled up like a watch <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Some were seen clothed in the same cloth used in the island of Otaheite, tinged of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> colour with turmeric; and these our voyagers supposed to be chiefs. Their colour is a chestnut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> black, curling, and remarkably strong; and that on the head as well as the face is cut short. The women are small, and slender limbed: they have punctures on the face, resembling the patches sometimes used by European ladies; they paint their face all over with a reddish brown ruddle, and above this they lay a fine orange colour extracted from turmeric root; the whole is then variegated with streaks of white shell lime. But the most surprising circumstance of all with regard to these people, is the apparent scarcity of women among them. The nicest calculation that could be made, never brought the number of inhabitants in this island to above 700, and of these the females bore no proportion in number to the males. Either they have but few females, or else their women were restrained from appearing during the stay of the ship; notwithstanding, the men showed no signs of a jealous disposition, or the women any scruples of appearing in public: in fact, they seemed to be neither revered nor chaste; and the large pointed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> which they wore gave them the appearance of professed wantons. But as all the women who were seen were liberal of their favours, it is more than probable that all the married and modest ones had concealed themselves from their impetuous visitants in some inextricable parts of the island; and what further strengthens this supposition is, that heaps of stones were seen piled up into little hillocks, which had one steep perpendicular side, where a hole went under ground. The space within, says Mr Forster, could be but small; and yet it is probable that these cavities served, together with their miserable huts, to give shelter to the people at night; and they may communicate with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> caverns, which are very common in the lava currents of volcanic countries. The few women that appeared were the most lascivious of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> perhaps that have been ever noticed in any country; shame seemed to be entirely unknown to them.

EATON

Pages 115-115

a town of Buckinghamshire, situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, opposite to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, and famous for its collegiate school, founded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VI. being a seminary for King's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, the fellows of which are all from this school. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETON">ETON</a>. EAU DE CARMES. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">PHARMACY</a>. Eau de Luce, a fragrant alkaline liquor which was some years ago in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> repute, especially among the fair <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and of which the leading perfection is, that it shall possess and retain a milky opacity. Mr Nicolson, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his valuable journal, tells us, that being informed by a philosophical friend, that the usual recipes for making this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> do not succeed, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of mastic in it has hitherto been kept a secret, he made the following trials to procure a good eau de luce. One dram of the rectified <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> was dissolved in four ounces of the strongest ardent spirit of the shops; its specific gravity being .840 at 60 degrees of Fahrenheit. A portion of the clear spirit was poured upon a larger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of fine powdered mastic than it was judged could be taken up. This was occasionally agitated without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; by which means the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> resin was for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> gradually dissolved. One part of the oily solution was poured into a phial, and to this was added one part of the solution of mastic. No opacity <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other change appeared. Four parts of strong caustic volatile alkali were then poured in, and immediately shaken. The fluid was of a dense opaque <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, affording a slight ruddy tinge when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> was seen through a thin portion of it. In a second mixture, four parts of the alkali were added to one of the solution of mastic; it appeared of a less dense and more yellowish white than the former mixture. More of the gum resinous solution was then poured in; but it still appeared less opaque than that mixture. It was ruddy by transmitted light. The last experiment was repeated with the oily solution instead of that of mastic. The white was much less dense than either of the foregoing compounds, and the requisite opacity was not given by augmenting the dose of the oily solution. No rudeness nor other remarkable appearance was seen by transmitted light. These mixtures were left at repose for two days; no separation appeared in either of the compounds containing mastic; the compound, consisting of the oily solution and alkali, became paler by the separation of a cream at the top. It appears, therefore, that the first of these three mixtures, subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the quantity of its ingredients, and the odorant additions which may be made, is a good eau de luce. In a subsequent number of the same Journal, we have the following recipe by one of the author's correspondents, who had often proved its value by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. "Digest ten or twelve grains of the whitest pieces of mastic, selected for this purpose and powdered, in two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a>; and, when nearly dissolved, add twenty grains of elemi. When both the resins are dissolved, add ten or fifteen drops of rectified oil of amber, and fifteen or twenty of essence of bergamot; shake the whole well together, and let the excess subside. The solution <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> amber colour. It is to be added in very small portions to the best <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">aqua</a> ammoniae purae, until it attains a milky whiteness, shaking the phial well after each addition, as directed by Macquer. The strength and causticity of the ammoniac are of most essential <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a>, upon the addition of the first drop or two of the tincture, a dense opaque congealed precipitate is formed, not much unlike that which appears on dropping a solution of silver into <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> slightly impregnated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, it is too strong, and must be diluted with alcohol. A considerable proportion of the tincture, perhaps one to four, ought to be employed to give the liquor the proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of opacity."

EAVES

Pages 115-115

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, the margin <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> edge of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; being the lowest tiles, slates, or the like, that hang over the walls, to throw off <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to a distance from the wall.

EAVES-DROPPERS

Pages 115-115

are such persons as stand under the eaves, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> walls, and windows of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, by night or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to hearken after news, and carry it to others, and thereby cause strife and contention in the neighbourhood. They are called evil members of the commonwealth by the stat. of West. i. c. 33. They may be punished either in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> leet by way of presentment and fine, or in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> sessions by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> and binding to good behaviour. EBBING OF THE <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">TIDES</a>. See TIDE.

EBDOMARIUS

Pages 115-115

in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writers, an officer formerly appointed weekly to superintend the performance of divine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in cathedrals, and prescribe the duties of each person attending in the choir, as to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">reading</a>, singing, praying, &c. To this purpose the ebdomary, at the beginning of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, drew up in form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> of the respective persons, and their several offices, called tabula, and the persons there entered were styled intabulati.

EBDOME

Pages 115-115

ἐβδόμη, in antiquity, a festival kept on the seventh of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, to whom all seventh days were sacred, because one of them was his birth-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; whence he was sometimes called Ebdomagenes. For the ceremonies of this solemnity see Potter's Archæol. Græc. lib. ii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 20.

EBION

Pages 115-115

the author of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> of the EBIONITES, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Cerinthus, and his successor. He improved upon the errors of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, and added to them new opinions of his own. He began his preaching in Judea; he taught in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and even at Rome. His tenets infected the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Cyprus. St John opposed both Cerinthus and Ebion in Asia; and it is thought, that this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOSTLE">apostle</a> wrote his gospel, in the year 97, particularly against this heresy.

EBIONITES

Pages 115-116
ancient heretics, who rose in the church in the very first age thereof, and formed themselves into a sect in the second century, denying the divinity of Jesus Christ. Origen takes them to have been so called from the Hebrew word *ebion*, which in that language signifies poor; because, says he, they were poor in sense, and wanted understanding. Eusebius, with a view to the same etymology, is of opinion they were thus called, as having poor thoughts of Jesus Christ, taking him for no more than a mere man. It is more probable the Jews gave this appellation to the Christians in general out of contempt; because in the first times there were few but poor people that embraced the Christian religion. This opinion Origen himself seems to give into, in his book against Celsus, where he says that they called Ebionites, such among the Jews as believed that Jesus was truly the expected Messiah. It might even be urged, with some probability, that the primitive Christians assumed the name themselves, in conformity to their profession. It is certain, Epiphanius observes, they valued themselves on being poor, in imitation of the apostles. The same Epiphanius, however, is of opinion, that there had been a man of the name of Ebion, the chief and founder of the sect of Ebionites, contemporary with the Nazarenes and Cerinthians. He gives a long and exact account of the origin of the Ebionites, making them to have risen after the destruction of Jerusalem, when the first Christians, called Nazarenes, went out of the same to live at Pella. The Ebionites were little else than a branch of Nazarenes: only that they altered and corrupted in many things the purity of the faith held among those first adherents to Christianity. For this reason Origen distinguishes two kinds of Ebionites, in his answer to Celsus; the one believed that Jesus Christ was born of a virgin; and the other, that he was born after the manner of other men. The first were orthodox in every thing, except that to the Christian doctrine they joined the ceremonies of the Jewish law, with the Jews, Samaritans, and Nazarenes; together with the traditions of the Pharisees. They differed from the Nazarenes, however, in several things, chiefly as to what regards the authority of the sacred writings; for the Nazarenes received all for Scripture contained in the Jewish canon; whereas the Ebionites rejected all the prophets, and held the very names of David, Solomon, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel, in abhorrence. They also rejected all St Paul's epistles, whom they treated with the utmost disrespect. They received nothing of the Old Testament but the Pentateuch; which should intimate them to have descended rather from the Samaritans than from the Jews. They agreed with the Nazarenes in using the Hebrew gospel of St Matthew, otherwise called the Gospel of the Twelve Apostles; but they had corrupted their copy in abundance of places; and particularly, had left out the genealogy of our Saviour, which was preserved entire in that of the Nazarenes, and even in those used by the Cerinthians. Some, however, have made this gospel canonical, and of greater value than our present Greek gospel of St Matthew: See Nazarenes. These last, whose sentiments, as to the birth of our Saviour, were the same with those of the Ebionites, built their error on this very genealogy. Besides the Hebrew gospel of St Matthew, the Ebionites had adopted several other books, under the names of St James, John, and the other apostles: they also made use of the Travels of St Peter, which are supposed to have been written by St Clement; but had altered them so, that there was scarce any thing of truth left in them. They even made that faint tell a number of falsehoods, the better to authorize their own practices. See St Epiphanius, who is very diffusive on the ancient heresy of the Ebionites, Hier. 30. But his account deserves little credit, as, by his own confession, he has confounded the other sects with the Ebionites, and has charged them with errors to which the first adherents of this sect were utter strangers. EBONY OF CRETE. See EBENUS, BOTANY Index. EBONY Wood is brought from the Indies, exceedingly hard and heavy, susceptible of a very fine polish, and on that account used in mosaic and inlaid works, toys, &c. There are divers kinds of ebony; the most usual among us are black, red, and green, all of them the product of the island of Madagascar, where the natives call them differently *hason mainthi*, q. d. black wood. The island of St Maurice, belonging to the Dutch, likewise furnishes part of the ebonies used in Europe. Authors and travellers give very different accounts of the tree that yields the black ebony. By some of their descriptions, it should be a sort of palm tree; by others a cytus, &c. The most authentic of them is that of M. Falcourt, who resided many years in Madagascar as governor thereof; he affirms us, that it grows very high and big, its bark being black, and its leaves resembling those of our myrtle, of a deep dusky green colour. Tavernier affirms us, that the islanders always take care to bury their trees, when cut down, to make them the blacker, and to prevent their splitting when wrought. F. Plumier mentions another black ebony tree, discovered by him at St Domingo, which he calls *portunum portulaceae foliis aculeatum ebeni materie*. Candia also bears a little shrub, known to the botanists under the name of *Ebenus Cretica*, above described. Pliny and Dioscorides say the best ebony comes from Ethiopia, and the worst from India; but Theophratus prefers that of India. Black ebony is much preferred to that of other colours. The best is a jet black, free of veins and rind, very massive, astringent, and of an acrid pungent taste. Its rind, infused in water, is said to purge pituita, and cure venereal disorders; whence Matthiolus took guaiacum for a sort of ebony. It yields an agreeable perfume when laid on burning coals; when green, it readily takes fire from the abundance of its fat. If rubbed against a stone, it becomes brown. The Indians make statues of their gods, and sceptres for their princes, of this wood. It was first brought to Rome by Pompey, after he subdued Mithridates. It is now much less used among us than anciently, since the discovery of so many ways of giving other hard woods a black colour. As to the green ebony, besides Madagascar and St Maurice, it likewise grows in the Antilles, and especially in the isle of Tobago. The tree that yields it is very bushy; its leaves are smooth, and of a fine green colour. Beneath its bark is a white blea, about two inches thick; all beneath which, to the very heart, is a deep green, approaching towards a black, though sometimes streaked with yellow veins. Its use is not confined

EBORACUM

Pages 116-117

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a famous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of the Brigantes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, the residence of Septimius Severus and Constantius Chlorus, and where they both died; a Roman colony; and the station of the Legio Sexta Victrix. Now <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 50. Lat. 54. Caer-frock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Caer-effroc, in British (Camden).

EBUDE

Pages 117-117
or Hebudes, in Ancient Geography, islands on the west of Scotland. The ancients differ greatly as to their situation, number and names; said in general to lie to the north of Ireland and west of Scotland. Now called the Western Isles, also Hebrides; this last a modern name, the reason of which does not appear, unless it be a corruption of Hebudes. By Beda called Mevanier, an appellation equally obscure.

EBULLITION

Pages 117-117

the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">Boiling</a>. The word is also used in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> with Effervescence.

EBUSUS

Pages 117-117

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the greater of the two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> called Pityuza, in the Mediterranean, near the east <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, to the south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>. Famous for its pastures for cattle, and for its figs. Now Ibiza, 100 miles in compass, without any noxious animals but rabbits, who often destroy the corn.

ECALESIA

Pages 117-117

Exalharia, in antiquity, a festival kept in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, named Hecules, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Hecalephus, from Hecale, one of the borough <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>.

ECASTOR

Pages 117-117

in antiquity, an oath wherein <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> was invoked. It was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> for the men never to swear by Castor, nor the women by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a>.

ECATEA

Pages 117-117

Exalharia, in antiquity, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> erected to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Hecate, for whom the Athenians had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> veneration, believing that she was the overseer of their families, and that she protected their children.

ECATESIA

Pages 117-117

Exalharia, in antiquity, an anniversary solemnity, observed by the Stratonicenians, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Hecate. The Athenians likewise had a public entertainment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a> every new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, in honour of the same <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. The supper was provided at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the richer sort; and was no sooner brought to the accustomed <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> people carried all off, giving out that Hecate had devoured it. For the rest of the ceremonies observed on this occasion, see Pott. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">Arch</a>. Grec. lib. ii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 20. ECATOMBÆON, Exalharia, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">Chronology</a>, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year. It consisted of 30 days, and began on the first new moon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice, and consequently answered to the latter Ecatombeion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> and beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. The Boeotians called it Hippodromus, and the Macedonians Louros. See Month. The word is a derivative from the Greek ἑκατόν, a hecatomb, because of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of hecatombs sacrificed in it.

ECAVESSADE

Pages 117-117

in the manege, is used for a jerk of the cavellon.

ECBATANA

Pages 117-117

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> residence and the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Media, built by Deioces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Medes, according to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>: Pliny says, by Seleucus; but that could not be, because it is mentioned by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOSTHENES">Demosthenes</a>. It was situated on a gentle declivity, distant 12 stadia from Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORONTES">Orontes</a>, and was in compass 50 stadia. Here stood the royal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> and tombs. It was an open walled town, but had a very strong citadel, encompassed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> walls, one within and rising above another. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the outmost was equal to the whole extent of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, according to Herodotus; the situation favouring this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, as being a gentle ascent, and each wall was of a different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>.—Another Ecbatana of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGI">Magi</a> (Pliny).—A third of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. ECCENTRICITY. See EXCENTRICITY.

ECCLESIASTES

Pages 117-118

a canonical book of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of which is to show the vanity of all sublunary things. It was composed by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>; who enumerates the several <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> several objects on which men <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, and then shows the insufficiency of all worldly enjoyments. The Talmudists made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Hezekiah to be the author of it: Grotius ascribes it to Zorobabel, and others to Isaiah; but the generality of commentators believe this book to be the produce of Solomon's <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>, after having experienced all the follies and pleasures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>.

ECCLESIASTICAL

Pages 118-119

an appellation given to whatever belongs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>: thus we say, ecclesiastical polity, jurisdiction, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, &c. Blackstone's Comments Ecclesiastical Courts. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Anglo-Saxons there was no sort of distinction between the lay and the ecclesiastical jurisdiction: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> was as much a spiritual as a temporal tribunal: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the church were ascertained and affected at the same time, and by the same judges, as the rights of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>. For this purpose the bishop of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in his absence the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the county, used to sit together in the county court, and had there the cognizance of all causes as well ecclesiastical as civil; a superior deference being paid to the bishop's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> in spiritual matters, and to that of the lay judges in temporal. This union of power was very advantageous to them both: the presence of the bishop added <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and reverence to the sheriff's proceedings; and the authority of the sheriff was equally useful to the bishop, by enforcing obedience to his decrees in such refractory offenders as would otherwise have despised the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> ecclesiastical censures. But so moderate and rational a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was wholly inconsistent with those views of ambition that were then forming by the court of Rome. It soon became an established maxim in the papal system of policy, that all ecclesiastical persons, and all ecclesiastical causes, should be solely and entirely subject to ecclesiastical jurisdiction only: which jurisdiction was supposed to be lodged in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> and immediately in the Pope, by divine indefeasible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTITURE">investiture</a> from Christ himself, and derived from the Pope to all inferior tribunals. Hence the canon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> lays it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> as a rule, that "facere deos a regibus honorandi sunt, non judicandi;" and places an emphatical reliance on a fabulous tale which it tells of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Constantine. That when some petitions were brought to him, imploring the aid of his authority against certain of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> accused of oppression and injustice; he caused, (says the holy canon) the petitions to be burnt in their presence, dismissing them with this valediction: "Ite, et inter vos causae vestras discutite, quia dignum non est ut nos judicemus Deos." It was not, however, till after the Norman conquest, that this doctrine was received in England; when William I. (whose <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> was warmly espoused by the monasteries which he liberally endowed, and by the foreign clergy whom he brought over in shoals from France and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and planted in the best preferments of the English church) was at length prevailed upon to establish this fatal encroachment, and separate the ecclesiastical court from the civil: whether actuated by principles of bigotry, or by those of a more refined policy, in order to discountenance the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Edward abounding with the spirit of Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, is not altogether certain. But the latter, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not the cause, Ecclesiastical was undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, of this separation: for the Saxon laws were soon overborne by the Norman justiciaries, when the county court fell into disrepute by the bishop's withdrawing his presence, in obedience to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of the conqueror; which prohibited any spiritual cause from being tried in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> courts, and commanded the suitors to appear before the bishop only, whose decisions were directed to conform to the canon law. King Henry I. at his accession, among other restorations of the laws of King Edward the Confessor, revived this of the union of the civil and ecclesiastical courts. Which was, according to Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the conquest was past, only a restitution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> law of England. This however was ill relished by the Popish clergy, who, under the guidance of that arrogant prelate Archbishop <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANSELM">Anselm</a>, very early disapproved of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> that put them on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the profane laity, and subjected spiritual men and causes to the inspection of the secular magistrates: and therefore, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNOD">synod</a> at Westminster, 3 Hen. I. they ordained, that no bishop should attend the discussion of temporal causes; which soon dissolved this newly effected union. And, when upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of King Henry I. the usurper Stephen was brought in and supported by the clergy, we find one article of the oath which they imposed upon him was, that ecclesiastical persons and ecclesiastical causes should be subject only to the bishop's jurisdiction. And as it was about that time that the contest and emulation began between the laws of England and those of Rome, the temporal courts adhering to the former, and the spiritual adopting the latter, as their rule of proceeding; this widened the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> between them, and made a coalition afterwards impracticable; which probably would else have been effected at the general reformation of the church. Ecclesiastical courts are various; as the Archdeacons', the Consistory, the court of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">Arches</a>, the Peculiars, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">Prerogative</a>, and the great court of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> in all ecclesiastical causes, viz. the Court of Delegates. See these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. As to the method of proceeding in the spiritual courts, it must (in the first place) be acknowledged to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, that though they continue to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to decide many questions which are properly of temporal cognizance, yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is in general so able and impartially administered, in those tribunals (especially of the superior kind), and the boundaries of their power are now so well known and established, that no material inconvenience at present arises from this jurisdiction still continuing in the ancient channel. And, should any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> be attempted, great confusion would probably arise, in overturning <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> established forms, and new-modelling a course of proceedings that has now prevailed for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> centuries. The establishment of the civil law <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in all the ecclesiastical courts was indeed a masterpiece of papal dexterity, as it made a coalition impracticable between them and the national tribunals, without manifest inconvenience and hazard. And this consideration had undoubtedly its weight in causing this measure to be adopted, though many other causes concurred. In particular, it may be here remarked, that the Pandects, or Ecclesiastical Corporations, are where the members that compose them are spiritual persons. They were erected for the furtherance of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and perpetuating the rights of the church. See Corporations. Ecclesiastic State. See Clergy. Ecclesiasticus, an apocryphal book, generally bound up with the Scriptures; so called, from its being read in the church, ecclesia, as a book of piety and instruction, but not of infallible authority. The author of this book was a Jew, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> the son of Sirach. The Greeks call it the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> of the son of Sirach. Eccoptics, in Medicine, laxative or loofening remedies, which purge gently, by softening the humours and excrements, and fitting them for expulsion.—The word is composed of the Greek particle εκ, and κοπτειν, excriment. Ecdici, ecdicii, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, patrons of cities, who defended their rights, and took care of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. Their office resembled that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> syndics. Echape, in the manege, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> begot between a stallion and a mare of different breeds and countries. Echaper, in the manege, a gallicism used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, implying to give a horse head, or to put on at full speed. Echeneis, the Remora. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Echevin, in the French and Dutch polity, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a> elected by the inhabitants of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town, to take care of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> concerns, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECORATION">decoration</a> and cleanliness of the city. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, there is a prevôt and four echevins; in other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, a mayor and echevins. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMSTERDAM">Amsterdam</a>, there are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> echevins; and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, seven. In France, the echevins take cognizance of rents, taxes, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, they judge of civil and criminal causes; and if the criminal confesses himself guilty, they can see their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> executed without appeal. Echinate, or Echinated, an appellation given to whatever is prickly, thereby resembling the hedgehog. Echinites, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> History, the name by which authors call the foxtail centronia, frequently found in our chalk pits. Echinophora. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Echinops. See Botany Index. Echinus,

ECHELLENSIS

Pages 117-117
ABRAHAM, a learned Maronite, whom the president Le Jai employed in the edition of his Polyglott Bible. Gabriel Sionita, his countryman, drew him to Paris, in order to make him his fellow labourer in publishing that Bible. They fell out; Gabriel complained to the parliament, and cruelly defamed his associate; their quarrel made a great noise. The congregation de propaganda fide afflicated him, 1636, with those whom they employed in making an Arabic translation of the Scriptures. They recalled him from Paris, and he laboured in that translation at Rome in the year 1652. While he was professor of the Oriental languages at Rome, he was pitched upon by the great duke Ferdinand II. to translate from Arabic into Latin the 5th, 6th, and 7th books of Apollonius's Conics; in which he was assisted by John Alphonso Borelli, who added commentaries to them. He died at Rome in 1644.

ECHINUS

Pages 120-120

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a member <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ornament near the bottom of the Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite capitals. ECHITES. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ECHO

Pages 120-121
or ECCHO, a sound reflected or reverberated, from a solid, concave, body, and so repeated to the ear. The word is formed from the Greek ἑχώ, ἑχεῖν, ἑχοῦσιν, ἑχοῦσιν. The ancients being wholly unacquainted with the true cause of the echo, ascribed it to several causes sufficiently whimsical. The poets, who were not the worst of their philosophers, imagined it to be a person of that name metamorphosed, and that the affected to take up her abode in particular places; for they found by experience, that she was not to be met with in all. (See below, Echo in Fabulous History.) But the moderns, who know sound to consist in a certain tremor or vibration in the sonorous body communicated to the contiguous air, and by that means to the ear, give a more consistent account of echo. For a tremulous body, striking on another solid body, it is evident, may be repelled without destroying or diminishing its tremor; and consequently a sound may be redoubled by the reflection of the tremulous body, or air. But a simple reflection of the sonorous air is not enough to solve the echo: for then every plain surface of a solid hard body, as being fit to reflect a voice or sound, would redouble it; which we find does not hold. To produce an echo, therefore, it should seem that a kind of concameration or vaulting were necessary, in order to collect, and by collecting to heighten and increase, and afterwards reflect, the sound; as we find is the case in reflecting the rays of light, where a concave mirror is required. In effect, as often as a sound strikes perpendicularly on a wall, behind which is any thing of a vault or arch, or even another parallel wall, so often will it be reverberated in the same line, or other adjacent ones. For an echo to be heard, therefore, it is necessary the ear be in the line of reflection: for the person who made the sound to hear its echo, it is necessary he be perpendicular to the place which reflects it; and for a manifold or tautological echo, it is necessary there be a number of walls, and vaults or cavities, either placed behind or fronting each other. A single arch or concavity, &c. can scarce ever stop and reflect all the sound; but if there be a convenient disposition behind it, part of the sound propagated thither, being collected and reflected as before, will present another echo: or, if there be another concavity, opposed at a due distance to the former, the sound reflected from the one upon the other will be tossed back again by this latter, &c. Many of the phenomena of echoes are well considered by the bishop of Leighs, &c. who remarks, that any sound, falling either directly or obliquely on any dense body of a smooth, whether plain or arched, superficies, is reflected, or echoes, more or less. The surface, says he, must be smooth; otherwise the air, by reverberation, will be put out of its regular motion, and the sound thereby broken and extinguished. He adds, that it echoes more or less, to show, that when all things are as before described, there is still an echoing, though it be not always heard, either because the direct sound is too weak to beat quite back again to him that made it; or that it does return to him, but so weak, that it cannot be discerned; or that he stands in a wrong place to receive the reflected sound, which passes over his head, under his feet, or on one side of him; and which therefore may be heard by a man standing in the place where the reflected sound does come, provided no interposed body intercepts it, but not by him that first made it. Echoes may be produced with different circumstances. For, 1. A plane obstacle reflects the sound back in its due tone and loudness; allowance being made for the proportionable decrease of the sound, according to its distance. 2. A convex obstacle reflects the sound somewhat smaller and somewhat quicker, though weaker, than otherwise it would be. 3. A concave obstacle echoes back the sound, bigger, flower, and also inverted; but never according to the order of words. Nor does it seem possible to contrive any single echo, that shall invert the sound, and repeat backwards; because, in such case, the word last spoken, that is, which last occurs to the obstacle, must be repelled first; which cannot be. For where in the mean time should the first words hang and be concealed? or how, after such a pause, be revived, and animated again into motion? From the determinate concavity or archness of the reflecting bodies, it may happen that some of them shall only echo back one determinate note, and only from one place. 4. The echoing body being removed farther off, it reflects more of the sound than when nearer; which is the reason why some echoes repeat but one syllable, some one word, and some many. 5. Echoing bodies may be so contrived and placed, as that reflecting the sound from one to the other, either directly and mutually, or obliquely and by succession, out of one sound, a multiple echo or many echoes shall arise. Add, that a multiple echo may be made, by so placing the echoing bodies at unequal distances, that they may reflect all one way, and not one on the other; by which means, a manifold successive sound will be heard; one clap of the hands, like many; one ha, like a laughter; one single word, like many of the same tone and accent; and so one viol, like many of the same kind, imitating each other. Lastly, Echoing bodies may be so ordered, that from any one sound given, they shall produce many echoes different both as to tone and intention. By which means a musical room may be so contrived, that not only one instrument playing therein shall seem many of the same fort and size, but even a concert of different ones, only by placing certain echoing bodies so, that any note played shall be returned by them in 3ds, 6ths, and 8ths. Echo, is also used for the place where the repetition of the sound is produced or heard. Echoes are distinguished into divers kinds, viz. 1. Single, 1. Single, which return the voice but once. Whereof some are tonical, which only return a voice when modulated into some particular musical tone: Others, polyphallic, which return many syllables, words, and sentences. Of this last kind is that fine echo in Woodstock park, which Dr Plot affirms us, in the day time, will return very distinctly seventeen syllables, and in the night twenty. 2. Multiple, or tautological; which return syllables and words the same oftentimes repeated. In echoes, the place where the speaker stands is called the centrum phonicum, and the object or place that returns the voice, the centrum phonoacanticum. At the sepulchre of Metella, wife of Craflus, was an echo, which repeated what a man said five times. Authors mention a tower at Cyzicus, where the echo repeated seven times. One of the finest echoes we read of is that mentioned by Barthius, in his notes on Statius's Thebaïs, lib. vi. 90, which repeated the words a man uttered 17 times: it was on the banks of the Naha, between Coblenz and Bingen. Barthius affirms us, he had proved what he writes; and had told 17 repetitions. And whereas, in common echoes, the repetition is not heard till some time after hearing the word spoke, or the notes sung; in this, the person who speaks or sings is scarce heard at all; but the repetition most clearly, and always in surprising varieties; the echo seeming sometimes to approach nearer, and sometimes to be further off. Sometimes the voice is heard very distinctly, and sometimes scarce at all. One hears only one voice, and another several; one hears the echo on the right, and the other on the left, &c. At Milan in Italy, is an echo which reiterates the report of a pistol 56 times; and if the report is very loud, upwards of 60 reiterations may be counted. The first 20 echoes are pretty distinct; but as the noise seems to fly away, and answer at a greater distance, the reiterations are so doubled, that they can scarce be counted. See an account of a remarkable echo under the article Paisley. Echo, in Architecture, a term applied to certain kinds of vaults and arches, most commonly of the elliptic and parabolic figures, used to redouble sounds, and produce artificial echoes. Echo, in Poetry, a kind of composition wherein the last words or syllables of each verse contain some meaning, which, being repeated apart, answers to some question or other matter contained in the verse; as in this beautiful one from Virgil: Crudelis mater magis, an puer improbus ille? Improbus ille puer, crudelis tu quoque mater. The elegance of an echo consists in giving a new sense to the last words; which reverberate, as it were, the motions of the mind, and by that means affect it with surprise and admiration. Echo, in fabulous history, a daughter of the Air and Tellus, who chiefly resided in the vicinity of the Cephalus. She was once one of Juno's attendants, and became the confidant of Jupiter's amours. Her loquacity, however, displeased Jupiter, and she was deprived of the power of speech by Juno, and only permitted to answer to the questions which were put to her. Pan had formerly been one of her admirers, but he never enjoyed her favours. Echo, after she had been punished by Juno, fell in love with Narcissus; but EchoMeter being despised by him, pined herself to death, having nothing but her voice left.

ECHOMETER

Pages 121-121

among musicians, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rule, with several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> thereon, serving to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and length of sounds, and to find their intervals and ratios. ECHOUERIES. See under Trichacus.

ECHYMOSIS

Pages 117-117

from εχύμειν, to pour out, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from εχύμη, out of, and χυμός, juice. It is an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EFFUSION">effusion</a> of humours from their respective vessels, under the integuments; or, as Paulus Aegneta says, "When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is bruised by the violent collision of any object, and its small veins broken, the blood is gradually discharged from them." This blood, when collected under the skin, is called echymosis; the skin in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> remaining entire; sometimes a tumour is formed by it, which is soft and livid, and generally without pain. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of blood is not considerable, it is usually reforbed; if much, it suppurates: it rarely happens that any further inconvenience follows; though, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a very bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of body, a mortification may be the result, and in such case regard must be had thereto. ECCLAIRCISSEMENT. See ESCLAIRCISSEMENT.

ECKIUS

Pages 121-121

John, an eminent and learned divine, professor in the university of Ingolstadt, memorable for the opposition he gave to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>, Melanchthon, Caralofadius, and other leading <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> in Germany. He wrote many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLEMICAL">polemical</a> tracts; and among the rest, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUAL">Manual</a> of Controversies, printed in 1535, in which he discourses upon most of the heads contested between the Protestants and Papists. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of uncommon learning, parts, and zeal, and died in 1543.

ECLECTICS

Pages 121-121

a name given to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers, who, without attaching themselves to any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, took what they judged good and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> from each. Hence their denomination; which, in the original Greek, signifies, "that may be chosen," <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> "that chooses;" of the verb ελέγχω, I choose.—Laertius notes, that they were also, for the same reason denominated analogetici; but that they call themselves Philalethi, i.e., lovers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> or founder of the eclectic was one Potamon of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, who lived under Augustus and Tiberius; and who, weary of doubting of all things with the Sceptics and Pyrrhonians, formed the eclectic sect; which Vossius calls the eclectic. Towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> century, a sect arose in the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> under the denomination of Eclectic, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> Platonics. They professed to make truth the only object of their inquiry, and to be ready to adopt from all the different systems and sects such tenets as they thought agreeable to it.—However, they preferred <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> to the other philosophers, and looked upon his opinions concerning God, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and things invisible, as conformable to the spirit and genius of the Christian doctrine. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> patrons of this system was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMMONIUS">Ammonius</a> Saccas, who at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> laid the foundation of that sect, afterwards distinguished by the name of the new Platonics, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIAN">Alexandrian</a> school. See Ammonius and Platonists. Eclectics were also a certain set of physicians among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, of whom Archigenes, under Trajan, was the chief, who selected from the opinions of all the other sects that which appeared to them best and most rational; hence they are called eclectics, and their prescriptions medicina eclectic.

ECLIPSE

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle on the terrestrial globe, not only answering to, but falling within, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the celestial ecliptic. See Geography.

ECLIPTA

Pages 121-121

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of the polygamia superflua order, belonging to the syngenesia clas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The receptacle is chaffy; there is no pappus, and the corollule of the disk quadrifid.

ECLIPTIC

Pages 121-121

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> circle of the sphere, supposed to be drawn through the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, making an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the equinoctial of about

ECLOGUE

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>, a kind of pastoral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, wherein shepherds are introduced conversing together. The word is formed from the Greek εκλογή choice; so that, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>, eclogue should be no more than a select <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> choice piece; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> has determined it to a farther signification, viz. a little elegant composition in a simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> style and manner. Idyllion and eclogue, in their primary intention, are the same thing: thus, the idyllia, ἀδυνάτων, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a>, are pieces wrote perfectly in the same vein with the eclogae of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>. But custom has made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between them, and appropriated the name eclogue to pieces wherein shepherds are introduced speaking: idyllion, to those wrote like the eclogue, in a simple natural style, but without any shepherds in them.

ECLUSE

Pages 122-122

a small but strong town of the Dutch Low Countries, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, with a good harbour and sluices. The English besieged it in vain in 1405, and the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUGES">Bruges</a> in 1436. But the Dutch, commanded by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Maurice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>, took it in 1644. It is defended by several forts, and stands near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 10. N. Lat. 50. 25.

ECPHRACTICS

Pages 122-122

in Medicine, remedies which attenuate and remove obstructions. See Attenuants, and Deobstruents, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. ECSTASY. See Ecstasy.

ECSTATICI

Pages 122-122

Εκστατικοί, from εκστάσις, I am entranced, in antiquity, a kind of diviners who were <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into trances <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ecstasies, in which they lay like dead men, or asleep, deprived of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; but, after some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, returning to themselves, gave strange relations of what they had seen or heard.

ECTLIC

Pages 121-122

23° 30', which is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>'s greatest declination; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, more strictly speaking, it is that path or way among the fixed stars, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> appears to describe to an eye placed in the sun. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Some call it via Solis, "the way of the sun," because the sun in his apparent annual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> never deviates from it, as all the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> do more or less.

ECTROPIUM

Pages 122-122

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, is when the eyelids are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> retracted, so that they show their internal or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> surface, and cannot sufficiently cover the eye.

EDDA

Pages 122-123

in antiquities, is a system of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Icelandic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Runic <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MYTHOLOGY">mythology</a>, containing many curious particulars of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and manners, of the northern nations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>; or of the Scandinavians, who had migrated from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and from whom our Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> were descended. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a> apprehends that it was originally compiled, soon after the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> was abolished, as a course of poetical lectures, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of such young Icelanders as devoted themselves to the profession of a scald or poet. It consists of two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts; the first containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> system of mythology, properly called the Edda; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> being a kind of art of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and called scalda or poetics. The most ancient Edda was compiled by Soemund Sigfusson, named the Learned, who was born in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICELAND">Iceland</a> about the year 1057. This was abridged, and rendered more easy and intelligible about 120 years afterwards, by Snorro Sturlefon, who was supreme judge of Iceland in the years 1215 and 1222; and it was published in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. He added also the second <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the form of a dialogue, being a detail of different events transacted among the divinities. The only three pieces that are known to remain of the more ancient Edda of Soemund, are the Volupsa, the Havamal, and the Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>. The Volupsa, or prophecy of Vola or Fola, appears to be the text, on which the Edda is the comment. It contains, in two or three hundred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, the whole system of mythology disclosed in the Edda, and may be compared to the Sibylline verses, on account of its laconic yet bold style, and its imagery and obscurity. It is professedly a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> of the decrees of the Father of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the actions and operations of the gods. It describes the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHAOS">chaos</a>, the formation of the world, with its various inhabitants, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of the gods, their most signal adventures, their quarrels with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOKE">Loke</a> their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> adversary, and the vengeance that ensued; and concludes with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINAL">final</a> state of the universe, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> and conflagration, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the inferior deities and the evil beings, the renovation of the world, the happy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of the good, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of the wicked. The Havamal, or Sublime Discourse, is attributed to the god Odin, who is supposed to have given these precepts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> to mankind; it is comprised in about 120 stanzas, and resembles the book of Proverbs. Mr Mallet has given several extracts of this treatise on the Scandinavian ethics. The Runic chapter contains a short system of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a>, and especially of the enchantments wrought by the operation of Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, of which Mr Mallet has also given a specimen. A manuscript copy of the Edda of Snorro is preserved in the library of the university of Upsal; the first part of which hath been published with a Swedish and Latin version by M. Goranson. The Latin version is printed as a supplement to M. Mallet's Northern Antiquities. The first edition of the Edda was published by Reichenius, professor at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPENHAGEN">Copenhagen</a>, in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quarto volume, in the year Edda year 1665; containing the text of the Edda, a Latin translation by an Icelandic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>, a Danish version, and various readings from different MSS. M. Mallet has also given an English translation of the first part, accompanied with remarks; from which we learn, that the Edda teaches the doctrine of the Supreme, called the Universal Father, and Odin, who lives for ever, governs all his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, and directs the great things as well as the small; who formed the heaven, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and gave him a spirit or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, which shall live after the body shall have mouldered away; and then all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> shall dwell with him in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Gimle or Vingolf, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of friendship; but wicked men shall go to Hel, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and from thence to Niflheim, or the abode of the wicked, which is below in the ninth world. It inculcates also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of several inferior gods and goddesses, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of whom is Frigg or Freia, i.e. lady, meaning hereby the earth, who was the spouse of Odin or the Supreme God; whence we may infer that, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of these ancient philosophers, this Odin was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> principle or soul of the world, which uniting itself with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, had thereby put it into a condition to produce the intelligences or inferior gods, and men and all other creatures. The Edda likewise teaches the existence of an evil being called Loki, the calumniator of the gods, the artificer of fraud, who surpasses all other beings in cunning and perfidy. It teaches the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> of all things out of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSS">abyss</a> or chaos; the final destruction of the world by fire; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a> of the inferior divinities, both good and bad, into the bosom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, from whom all things proceeded, as emanations of his essence, and who <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> survive all things; and the renovation of the earth in an improved state.

EDDISH

Pages 123-123
or EADISH, the latter pasture or grass that comes after mowing or reaping; otherwise called engrafe or earfh, and etch.

EDDOES

Pages 123-123
or EDERS, in Botany, the American name of the Arum eculentum.

EDEN

Pages 123-123

(Moses) the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with a garden, in which the progenitors of mankind were settled by God himself: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> denotes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> delight. It would be endless to recount the several opinions concerning its situation, some of them very wild and extravagant. Moses says, that "a river went out of Eden to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> the garden, and from thence it was parted and became into four heads." This river is supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> channel of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> and Tigris, after their confluence; which parted again, below the garden, into two different channels; so that the two channels before, and the other two after their confluence, constitute the heads mentioned by Moses. Which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> determine the situation of the garden to have been in the south of Mesopotamia, or in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLONIA">Babylonia</a>. The garden was also called Paradise; a term of Persian origin, denoting a garden. See Paradise.

EDGINGS

Pages 123-123

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of small but durable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> set round the edges <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> borders of flower beds, &c. The best and most durable of all plants for this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is box; which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> well planted and rightly managed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> continue in strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> for many years. The seasons for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> this are the autumn, and very early in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>: and the best <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> for this purpose is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a> Dutch box. Formerly, it was also a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> practice to plant borders, or edgings, of aromatic herbs; as thyme, savory, hyssop, lavender, and the like; but these are all apt to grow woody, and to be in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, or wholly, destroyed in hard winters. Daisies, thrift, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> julyflower, and chamomile, are also used by some for this purpose; but they require yearly transplanting, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of trouble, else they grow out of form; and they are also subject to perish in very hard seasons.

EDHILLING

Pages 123-124

EDHILINGUS, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> appellation of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> among the Anglo-Saxons. The Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, says Nithard (Hist. lib. iv.) is divided into three orders <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> classes of people; the edhilingi, the frillingi, and the laezzi; which signify the nobility, the freemen, and the vassals or slaves. Instead of edhilling, we sometimes meet with atheling, or athelingi; which appellation was likewise given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s son, and the presumptive heir of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. See Athelling.

EDICT

Pages 124-124

in matters of polity, an order <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, signed and sealed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, to serve as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to his subjects. We find frequent mention of the edicts of the praetor, the ordinances of that officer in the Roman law. In the French law, the edicts are of several kinds: some importing a new law or regulation; others, the erection of new offices; establishments of duties, rents, &c.; and sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of pacification. In France, edicts are much the same as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> is with us: but with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the former have the authority of a law in themselves, from the power which issues them forth; whereas the latter are only declarations of a law, to which they refer, and have no power in themselves.

EDINBURGH

Pages 124-137

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mid-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTHIAN">Lothian</a> in Scotland, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3°, and N. Lat. 56°, near the southern <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the river Forth.—The origin of the name, like that of most other cities, is very uncertain.
