Plants of temperate climates, situated under the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> of latitude with certain parts of Europe, but removed much farther to the west, such as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>, do not produce flowers till autumn. Plants of temperate climates in the opposite hemisphere to Europe, flower during our winter, which is the summer of these regions. Linnaeus and Adanson have given a sketch of the different times in which plants flower at Upsal and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>.

EFFLUVIVM

Pages 199-199

in Physiology, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> much used by philosophers and physicians, to express the minute particles which exhale from moist, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not all, terrestrial bodies, in form of sensible vapours.

EFFRONTES

Pages 199-199

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of heretics, in 1534, who scraped their forehead with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> till it bled, and then poured <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> into the wound. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> served them instead of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. They are likewise said to have denied the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> of the Holy Spirit.

EFFUSION

Pages 199-199
or FUSION, in Astronomy, denotes that part of the sign Aquarius, represented on celestial globes and planispheres, by the water issuing out of the urn of the water-bearer.

EGERIA

Pages 199-199
or ÆGERIA, a nymph held in great veneration by the Romans. She was courted by Numa Pomilius; and, according to Ovid, she became his wife. This prince frequently visited her; and that he might introduce his laws and new regulations into the state, he solemnly declared before the Roman people, that they were previously sanctified and approved by the nymph Egeria. Ovid says, that Egeria was so disconsolate at the death of Numa, that she melted into tears, and was changed into a fountain by Diana. She is reckoned by many as a goddess who presided over the pregnancy of women; and some maintain that she is the same as Lucina.

EGG

Pages 199-200

in Physiology, a body formed in certain females, in which is contained an embryo <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fetus of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, under a cortical surface or shell. The exterior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of an egg is the shell; which in a hen, for instance, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, thin, and friable cortex, including all the other parts. The shell becomes more brittle by being exposed to a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>. It is lined everywhere with a very thin but a pretty tough membrane, which dividing at, or very near, the obtuse end of the egg, forms a small bag, where only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is contained. In new laid eggs this follicle appears very little, but becomes larger when the egg is kept. Within this are contained the albumen or white, and the vitellus or yolk; each of which have their different virtues. The albumen is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, viscid, white liquor in the egg, different in consistence in its different parts. It is observed, that there are two distinct albumens, each of which is enclosed in its proper membrane. Of these one is very thin and liquid; the other is more dense and viscous, and of a somewhat whiter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; but, in old and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> eggs, after some days incubation, inclining to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. As this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> albumen covers the yolk on all sides, so it is itself surrounded by the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> liquid. The albumen of a fecundated egg is as sweet and free from corruption, during all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of incubation, as it is in new laid eggs; as is also the vitellus. As the eggs of hens consist of two liquors separated one from another, and distinguished by two branches of umbilical veins, one of which goes to the vitellus, and the other to the albumen; so it is very probable that they are of different natures, and consequently appointed for different purposes. When the vitellus grows warm with incubation, it becomes more humid, and like melting wax or fat; whence it takes up more space. For as the fetus increases, the albumen insensibly wastes away and condenses; the vitellus, on the contrary, seems to lose little or nothing of its bulk when the fetus is perfected, and only appears more liquid and humid when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> of the fetus begins to be formed. The chick in the egg is first nourished by the albumen; and when this is consumed, by the vitellus, as with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we compare the chalaza to the extremities of an axis passing through the vitellus, which is of a spherical form, this sphere <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be composed of two unequal portions, its axis not passing through its centre; consequently, since it is heavier than the white, its smaller portion must always be uppermost in all positions of the egg. The yellowish white round spot, called cicatricula, is placed on the middle of the smaller portion of the yolk; and therefore, from what has been said in the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAGRAPH">paragraph</a>, must always appear on the superior part of the vitellus. Not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a> of the chick, the whole yolk is taken into its abdomen; and the shell, at the obtuse end of the egg, frequently appears cracked some time before the exclusion of the chick. The chick is sometimes observed to perforate the shell with its its beak. After exclusion, the yolk is gradually wasted, being conveyed into the small guts by a small duct. Eggs differ very much according to the birds that lay them, as to their colour, form, bigness, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and the different way of dressing them: those most used in food are hens eggs; of which, such as are new laid are best. As to the preservation of eggs, it is observed that the egg is always quite full when it is first laid by the hen; but from that time it gradually becomes less and less so, to its decay: and however <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> its shell may appear, it is nevertheless perforated with a multitude of small holes, though too minute for the discernment of our eyes, the effect of which is a daily decrease of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> within the egg, from the time of its being laid; and the perspiration is much quicker in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> than in cold. To preserve the egg fresh, there needs no more than to preserve it full, and stop its transpiration; the method of doing which is, by stopping up those pores with matter which is not soluble in watery <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>: and on this principle it is, that all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a>, prepared with spirit of wine, will preserve eggs fresh for a long time, if they are carefully rubbed all over the shell: tallow, or mutton fat, is also good for this purpose; for such as are rubbed over with this, will keep as long as those coated over with varnish. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Method of Hatching Eggs. See HATCHING. EGINA. See AEGINA.

EGINIART

Pages 200-200

secretary to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, was a German. He is the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> historian of that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, and wrote very eloquently for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of the 9th century. It is said, that he inflamed himself so well into the favour of Emma, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> to Charles the Great, that he obtained from her whatever he desired. Charles the Great, having found out the intrigue, did not do as Augustus, who is thought to have banished Ovid because he believed him to be too much favoured by Julia; for he married the two lovers together, and gave them a fine estate in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. EGLANTINE. See ROSA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

EGLON

Pages 200-200

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Moabites, who oppressed the Israelites for 18 years (Judges iii. 12—14). Calmet confounds this servitude of the Hebrews with that under Chushan-rishathaim, making it to subsist only eight years, from the year of the world 2591 to 2599; whereas this servitude under Eglon lasted 18 years, and commenced in the year of the world 2661, and 62 years after they had been delivered by Othniel from the subjection of Chushan-rishathaim.

EGRA

Pages 200-200

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, formerly imperial, but now subject to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. It contains a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of able artificers, and is famous for its mineral waters. Wallenstein, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s general, was affianced here in 1634. The French became masters of this town in 1741; but afterwards being blockaded up, they were forced to capitulate on September 7th, 1743. It is looked upon as a town of the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in Bohemia, except <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAGUE">Prague</a>. It is seated on a river of the same name, in L. Leng. 12. 30. N. Lat. 50. 21.

EGRET

Pages 200-200

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ardea. See ARDEA, ORNITHOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELAEOCARPUS

Pages 247-247

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandra clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELAEOTHESIUM

Pages 247-247

in antiquity, the anointing room, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where those who were to wrestle or had bathed anointed themselves. See Gymnasium.

ELAIS

Pages 247-247

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of Palmae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELAM

Pages 247-247

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> frequently mentioned in Scripture, and lying to the south-east of Shinar. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Daniel (viii. 2.), Sufiana seems to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it; and before the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, it does not appear that the Jews called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> by any other name. Elymae and Elymais are often mentioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, though he makes Elymais a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Media, yet he places the Elymae in Sufiana, near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. Stephanus takes it to be a part of Affrya; but Pliny and Jolephorus more properly of Persia, whose inhabitants this latter tells us sprang from the Elamites. The best commentators agree, that the Elamites, who were the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of the Persians, were descended from Elam the son of Shem. It is likewise allowed, that the most ancient among the inspired writers constantly intend Persia, when they speak of Elam and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Elam. Thus, not to detain the reader with unnecessary quotations, when the prophet Jeremiah (xlix. 39.), after denouncing many judgments against this country, adds these words, "But it shall come to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> in the latter days, that I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> bring again the captivity of Elam," <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>," he is always understood to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the restoration of the kingdom of the Persians by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYRUS">Cyrus</a>, who subdued the Babylonians, as they before had subdued the Persians.

ELAPHEBOLIA

Pages 247-247

in Grecian antiquity, a festival in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> the huntress. In the celebration a cake was made in the form of a deer (ἀλέπιον), and offered to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. It owed its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to the following circumstance: When the Thessalians had been severely beaten by the Thessalians, they resolved, by the perfusion of one Deiphantus, to raise a pile of combustible materials, and burn their wives, children, and effects, rather than submit to the enemy. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> was unanimously approved by the women, who decreed Deiphantus a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a>. When everything was prepared, before they fired the pile, they engaged their enemies, and fought with such desperate fury, that they totally routed them, and obtained a complete victory. In commemoration of this unexpected success, this festival was instituted to Diana, and observed with the greatest solemnity.

ELAPHEBOLIUM

Pages 247-247

in Grecian antiquity, the ninth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year, answering to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of February and beginning of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>. It consisted of 30 days; and took its name from the festival elaphebolia, kept in this month, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> the huntress, as mentioned in the preceding article.

ELASMIS

Pages 247-247

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a genus of talcs, composed of small plates in form of spangles; and either flingle, and not farther fliddle; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> complex, only flidle to a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, and that in somewhat thick laminae.—Of these tales there are several varieties, some with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and others with small spangles, which differ also in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and other peculiarities.

ELASTIC

Pages 247-249

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, an appellation given to all bodies endowed with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of elasticity. See Elasticity. ELASTIC <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">Air</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAS">Gas</a>, and Elastic Vapours below. ELASTIC Resin. See <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAOUTCHOUC">CAOUTCHOUC</a>. ELASTIC Vapours are such as may, by any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> force, be compressed into a smaller space than what they originally occupied; restoring themselves, when the pressure is taken off, to their former state with a force exactly proportioned to that with which they were at first compressed. Of this kind are all the aerial fluids without exception, and all kinds of fumes raised by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> whether from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fluid bodies. Of these, some retain their elasticity only when a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat is applied to them or the substance which produces them; while others remain elastic in every degree of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, either natural or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, that has yet been observed. Of the former kind are the vapours of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, spirit of wine, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, sal ammoniac, and all kinds of sublimable salts; of the latter, those of muriatic acid gas, hydrogen gas, nitrous gas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> air, &c. The elastic force with which any one of these fluids is endowed has not yet been calculated, as being ultimately greater than any obstacle we can put in its way. Thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we compress the atmospherical air, we shall find that for some little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> easily yield to the force we apply; but every succeeding moment the resistance will become stronger, and a greater and greater force must be applied in order to compress it further. As the compression goes on, the vessel containing the air becomes hot; but no power whatever has yet been able to destroy the elasticity of the contained fluid in any degree; for upon removing the pressure, it is always found to occupy the very same space that it did before. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is the same with aqueous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>, to which a sufficient heat is applied to keep it from condensing into water. This will yield to a certain degree; but every moment the resistance becomes greater, until at last it will overcome any obstacles whatever. An example of the power of this kind of steam we have every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> in the steam engine; and the vapours of other matters, both solid and fluid, have frequently manifested themselves to be endowed with an equal force. Thus the force of the vapours of spirit of wine has occasioned terrible accidents when the worm has been stopped, and the head of the still absurdly tied <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to prevent an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a>; the vapours of mercury have burnt an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> box; and those of sal ammoniac, volatile salts, nitrous acid, marine acid, phosphorus, &c., have all been known to burst the chemical vessels which confined them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force, in such a manner as to endanger those who stood near them. In short, from innumerable observations, it may be laid down as an undoubted fact, that there is no substance whatever capable of being reduced into a state of vapour, but what in that state is endowed with an elastic force ultimately superior to any obstacle we can throw in its way. It hath been a kind of desideratum among philosophers to give a satisfactory reason for this astonishing Elastic vapours, being power of elasticity in vapour, seemingly so little capable of accomplishing any great purpose when in an unconfined state. As air is that fluid in which, from the many experiments made upon it by the air-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> and otherwise, the elastic property has most frequently been observed, the researches of philosophers were at first principally directed towards it. The causes they assigned, however, were very inadequate; being founded upon a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a> concerning the form of the particles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> itself, which they supposed to be either rolled up like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of watches, or that they consisted of a kind of elastic flakes. This was followed by another hypothesis concerning their substance, which was imagined to be perfectly elastic, and so strong that they could not be broken by any mechanical power whatever; and thus they thought the phenomenon of the elasticity of the air might be explained. But an insuperable difficulty still attended their scheme, notwithstanding both these suppositions; for it was observed, that the elastic power of the air was augmented not only in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of pressure it was made to endure, but in proportion to the degree of heat applied to it at the time. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton was aware of this difficulty; and justly concluded, that the phenomena of the air's elasticity could not be solved on any other supposition but that of a repulsive power diffused all around each of its particles, which became stronger as they approached, and weaker as they removed from each other. Hence the common phenomena of the air-pump and condensing-engine received a satisfactory explanation; but still it remained to account for the power shown in the present case by heat, as it could not be denied that this element had a very great share in augmenting the elasticity of the atmosphere, and seemed to be the only cause of elasticity in other vapours. It does not appear that Sir Isaac entered into this question, but contented himself with attributing to heat the property of increasing repulsion, and ascribing this to another unexplored property called rarefaction. Thus matters stood till the great discovery made by Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a>, that some bodies have the power of absorbing in an unknown manner the element in question, and parting with it afterwards, so that it flows out of the body which had absorbed it with the very same properties that it had before <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSORPTION">absorption</a>. Hence many phenomena of heat, vapour, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>, were explained in a manner much more satisfactory than had ever been attempted or even expected before. One of these was that remarkable property of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> becoming hot by hammering; during which operation, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, the element of heat is squeezed out from between the particles of the metal, as water is from the pores of a sponge by pressing it between the fingers. Of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is the phenomenon above-mentioned, that air when violently compressed becomes hot, by reason of the quantity of more subtle element squeezed out from among the particles. In this manner it appears that heat and the repulsive power of Sir Isaac Newton are the very same; that by diminishing the heat of any quantity of air, its elasticity is effectually diminished, and it will of itself shrink into a smaller space as effectually as by mechanical pressure. In one case we have what may be called ocular demonstration of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of this doctrine, viz. that by throwing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of a strong <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENS">lens</a> upon a small quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> in vacuo, the whole will be converted into inflammable air, having even a greater power of elasticity than common air in an equal degree of heat. Here there is nothing else but heat or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> to produce the elastic power, or cause the particles of charcoal which before attracted now to repel each other. In another case we have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> equally strong, that the element of heat by itself, without the presence of that of light, is capable of producing the same effect. Thus when a phial of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a> is put into the receiver of an air pump, and surrounded by a small vessel of water, the ether boils violently, and is distilled in vapour, while the water freezes, and is cooled to a great degree. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of this vapour shows that it has an elastic force; and the absorption of the heat from the water shows, that this element not only produces the elasticity, but actually enters into the substance of the vapour itself; so that we have not the least reason to conclude that there is any other repulsive power by which the particles are kept at a distance from one another than the substance of the heat itself. In what manner it acts, we cannot pretend exactly to explain, without making hypotheses concerning the form of the minute particles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, which must always be very uncertain. All known phenomena, however, concur in rendering the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> now laid down extremely probable. The elasticity of the steam of water is exactly proportioned to the degree of heat which flows into it from without; and if this be kept up to a sufficient degree, there is no mechanical pressure which can reduce it into the state of water. This, however, may very easily be done by abstracting a certain portion of the latent heat it contains; when the elastic vapour will become a dense and heavy fluid. The same thing may be done in various ways with the permanently elastic fluids. Thus the purest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPHLOGISTICATED">dephlogisticated</a> air, when made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> with its latent heat by burning with iron, is converted into a gravitating substance of an unknown nature, which adheres strongly to the metal. If the decomposition is performed by means of inflammable air, both together unite into a heavy, aqueous, or acid fluid: if by mixture with nitrous air, still the heat is discernible, though less violent than in the two former <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. The decomposition indeed is slower, but equally complete, and the dephlogisticated air becomes part of the nitrous acid, from which it may be again expelled by proper means: but of these means heat must always be one; for thus only the elasticity can be restored, and the air be recovered in its proper state. The same thing takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in fixed air, and all other permanently elastic fluids capable of being absorbed by others. The conclusion therefore which we can only draw from what <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATA">data</a> we have concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of elastic vapours is, that all of them are formed of a terrestrial substance, united with the element of heat in such a manner that part of the latter may be squeezed out from among the terrestrial particles; but in such a manner, that as soon as the pressure is taken off, the surrounding fluid rushes in, and expands them to their original bulk: and this expansion or tendency to it will be increased in proportion to the degree of heat, just as the expansion of a sponge would be exceedingly augmented, if we could contrive to convey a stream of water into Elasticity into the heart of it, and make the liquid flow out with violence through every pore in the circumference. In this case, it is evident that the water would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a power of repulsion among the particles of the sponge, as well as the fire does among the particles of the water, charcoal, or whatever other substance is employed. Thus far we may reason from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a>; but in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the internal and essential texture of these vapors will forever remain unknown. Their obvious properties, as well as some of their more latent operations in many cases, are treated of under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. It has been imagined by some, that the artificial elastic fluids have not the same mechanical property with common air, viz. that of occupying a space inversely <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the weights with which they are pressed; but this is found to be a mistake. All of them likewise have been found to be non-conductors of electricity, though probably not all in the same degree. Even aqueous vapor, when intimately mingled with any permanently elastic fluid, refuses to conduct this fluid, as is evident from the highly electrical state of the atmosphere in very dry <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, when we are certain that aqueous vapor must abound very much, and be intimately mixed with it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the electric spark, though it may be made visible in all kinds of permanently elastic vapors, is very different in different fluids. Thus in inflammable and alkaline air it is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or purple, but in fixed air it appears <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>.

ELASTICITY

Pages 249-250
or Elastic Force, that property of bodies wherewith they restore themselves to their former figure, after any external pressure. The cause or principle of this important property elasticity, or springiness, is variously assigned. The Cartesians account for it from the materia subtilis making an effort to pass through pores that are too narrow for it. Thus, say they, in bending, or compressing, a hard elastic body, e.g., a bow, its parts recede from each other on the convex side, and approach on the concave; consequently the pores are contracted or tightened on the concave side; and if they were before round, are now, for instance, oval; so that the materia subtilis, or matter of the second element, endeavouring to pass out of those pores thus tightened, must make an effort, at the same time, to restore the body to the state it was in when the pores were more patent and round, i.e., before the bow was bent; and in this consists its elasticity. Other later and more wary philosophers account for elasticity much after the same manner as the Cartesians; with this only difference, that in lieu of the subtle matter of the Cartesians, these substitute Ether, or a fine ethereal medium that pervades all bodies. Others, setting aside the precarious notion of a materia subtilis, account for elasticity from the great law of nature attraction, or the cause of the cohesion of the parts of solid and firm bodies. Thus, say they, when a hard body is struck or bent, so that the component parts are moved a little from each other, but not quite disjointed or broke off, or separated so far as to be out of the power of that attractive force whereby they cohere; they must certainly, on the cessation of the external violence, spring back to their former natural state. Others resolve elasticity into the pressure of the atmosphere; for a violent tension or compression, though not so great as to separate the constituent particles of bodies far enough to let in any foreign matter, must yet occasion many little vacuums between the separated surfaces; so that upon the removal of the force they will close again by the pressure of the aerial fluid upon the external parts. See Atmosphere. Lastly, others attribute the elasticity of all hard bodies to the power of reflection in the air included within them; and so makes the elastic force of the air the principle of elasticity in all other bodies. The Elasticity of Fluids is accounted for from their particles being all endowed with a centrifugal force; when Sir Isaac Newton, prop. 23, lib. 2, demonstrates, that particles, which naturally avoid or fly off from one another by such forces as are reciprocally proportioned to the distances of their centre, will compose an elastic fluid, whose density shall be proportional to its compression; and vice versa, if any fluid be composed of particles that fly off and avoid one another, and hath its density proportional to its compression, then the centrifugal forces of those particles will be reciprocally as the distances of their centres. Elasticity of the Air, is the force wherewith that element dilates itself, upon removing the force whereby it was before compressed. See Air and Atmosphere. The elasticity or spring of the air was first discovered by Galileo. Its existence is proved by this experiment of that philosopher: An extraordinary quantity of air being intruded by means of a syringe into a glass or metal ball, till such time as the ball, with this accession of air, weighs considerably more in the balance than it did before; upon opening the mouth thereof, the air rushes out, till the ball sinks to its former weight. From hence we argue, that there is just as much air gone out, as compressed air had been crowded in. Air, therefore, returns to its former degree of expansion, upon removing the force that compressed or resisted its expansion; consequently it is endowed with an elastic force. It must be added, that as the air is found to rush out in every situation or direction of the orifice, the elastic force acts every way, or in every direction. The elasticity of the air makes a considerable article in Pneumatics. The cause of the elasticity of the atmosphere hath been commonly ascribed to a repulsion between its particles; but this can give us only a very slight idea of the nature of its elasticity. The term repulsion, like that of attraction, requires to be defined; and in all probability will be found in most cases to be the effect of the action of some other fluid. Thus, we find, that the elasticity of the atmosphere is very considerably affected by heat. Supposing a quantity of air heated to such a degree as is sufficient to raise Fahrenheit's thermometer to 212°, it will then occupy a considerable space. If it is cooled to such a degree as to sink the thermometer to 0°, it will shrink up into less than half the former bulk. The quantity of repulsive power power therefore acquired by the air, while passing from one of these states to the other, is evidently owing to the heat added or taken away from it. Nor have we any reason to suppose, that the quantity of elasticity or repulsive power it still possesses is owing to any other thing than the fire contained in it. The supposing repulsion to be a primary cause, independent of all others, hath given rise to many erroneous theories, and been one very great mean of embarrassing philosophers in their accounting for the phenomena of Electricity.

ELATE

Pages 250-250

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of Palmae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELATER

Pages 250-250

a genus of insects belonging to the order of Coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELATERIUM

Pages 250-250

Elaterium, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a violently purgative medicine, prepared from the wild cucumber.

ELATH

Pages 250-250
or Elath, a port of Idumaea, situated upon the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red sea, which David in his conquest of Edom took (2 Sam. viii. 14.), and there established a trade to all parts of the world. His son, we see, built ships in Elath, and sent them thence to Ophir for gold, (2 Chr. viii. 17, 18.). It continued in the possession of the Israelites about 150 years, till in the time of Joram, the Edomites recovered it (2 Kings viii. 20.); but it was again taken from them by Azariah, and by him left to his son, (2 Kings xiv. 22.). His grandson Ahaz, however, lost it again to the king of Syria (ib. xvi. 6.); and the Syrians had it in their hands a long while, till after many changes under the Ptolemies, it came at length into the possession of the Romans.

ELATINE
