a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the orchidaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELATOSTEMA

Pages 250-250

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocotyledons. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELBING

Pages 250-250

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Polish <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALATINATE">palatinate</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARIENBURG">Marienburg</a>, situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 20° 0' N. Lat. 54° 15', on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of the Baltic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, called the Frischeauff, near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VISTULA">Vistula</a>. The town is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, populous, and very well built. It is divided into two parts, called the old and new town, which are both of them very well fortified. The old town has a handsome tower, with a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. The stadt-haus and the academy are good buildings, with pleasant gardens, which are worth seeing. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> has a considerable trade, especially in sturgeon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAD">mead</a>, cheese, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and corn. It is seated in a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> like <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, very fruitful and populous. The inhabitants are partly Lutherans and partly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. The boors in the neighbourhood have as good houses and apparel almost as the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>.

ELBOW

Pages 250-250

the outer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> made by the flexure <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the arm. That eminence whereon the arm rests, called by us elbow, is by the Latins called cubitus, and the Greeks αγκών, and by others αγκώνας. Elbow is also used by architects, masons, &c., for an obtuse angle of a wall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a>, which diverts it from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line.

ELCESAITES

Pages 250-250

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> heretics, who made their appearance in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Trajan, and took their name from their leader Elcefaï. The Elcefaïtes kept a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> between the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, and Pagans; they worshipped but one God, observed the Jewish sabbath, circumcision, and the other ceremonies of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. They rejected the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENTATEUCH">Pentateuch</a>, and the prophets; nor had they any more respect for the writings of the apostles, particularly those of St Paul.

ELDERS

Pages 250-250
or Seniors, in Jewish history, were persons of the most considerable for age, experience, and wisdom. Of this sort were the 70 men whom Moses associated with himself in the government of his people; such, likewise, afterwards were those who held the first rank in the synagogue, as presidents. In the first assemblies of the primitive Christians, those who held the first place were called elders. The word presbyter, often used in the New Testament, is of the same signification; hence the first councils of Christians were called presbyteria, or councils of elders. Elders is also a denomination still retained in the Presbyterian discipline. The elders are officers, who, in conjunction with the pastors, or ministers, and deacons, compose the consistories or kirk-leissions, meeting to confer, inspect, and regulate, matters of religion and discipline. They are chosen from among the people, and are received publicly with some degree of ceremony. In Scotland, there is an indefinite number of elders in each parish; generally about 12. See Kirk-Leissions and Presbyteries. ELDER. See Sambucus, Botany Index.

ELEATIC PHILOSOPHY

Pages 250-251

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, a name given to that of the Stoics, because taught at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELEA">Elea</a>, in Latin Velia, a town of the Lucani. The founder of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the Eleatic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>, is supposed to have been Xenophanes, who lived about the 56th Olympiad, or between 500 or 600 years before Christ. This sect was divided into two parties, which may be denominated metaphysical and physical, the one rejecting, and the other approving, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to fact and experiment. Of the former kind were Xenophanes, Parmenides, Melissus, and Zeno of Elea. They are supposed to have maintained principles not very unlike those of Spinoza; they held the eternity and immutability of the world; that whatever existed was only one being; that there was neither any <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> nor corruption; that this one being was immoveable and immutable, and was the true God; and whatever changes seemed to happen in the universe, they considered as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> appearances and illusions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. However, some learned men have supposed, that Xenophanes and his followers, speaking metaphysically, understood by the universe, or the one being, not the material world, but the originating principle of of all things, or the true God, whom they expressly affirm to be incorporeal. Thus Simplicius represents them as merely metaphysical writers, who distinguished between things <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and supernatural; and who made the former to be compounded of different principles. Accordingly, Xenophanes maintained, that the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> consisted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and fire; that all things were produced out of the earth, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and stars out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, and that there were four elements. Parmenides also distinguished between the doctrine concerning metaphysical objects, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and that concerning physical or corporeal things, called <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; with respect to the former there was one immoveable principle, but in the latter two that were moveable, viz. fire and earth, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>; in which particulars Zeno agreed with him. The other branch of the Eleatic sect were the atomic philosophers, who formed their system from an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; of these the most considerable were Leucippus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOCRITUS">Democritus</a>, and Protagoras. ELECAMPANE. See INULA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

ELECT

Pages 251-251

(from eligo, "I choose") CHOSEN, in the Scriptures, is applied to the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, the elect are those chosen and admitted to the favour and blessing of Christianity. Elect, in some systems of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> appropriated to the saints, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the predestinated: in which sense the elect are those persons who are said to be predestinated to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> as the end, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANCTIFICATION">sanctification</a> as the means. Elect is likewise applied to archbishops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a>, and other officers, who are chosen, but not yet consecrated, or actually invested with their office or jurisdiction. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is said to be elect before he is inaugurated and crowned; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-mayor is elect, before his predecessor's mayoralty is expired, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> is put in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>.

ELECTION

Pages 251-255

in British polity, is the people's choice of their representatives in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. (See PARLIAMENT.) In this consists the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of the democratical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>: for in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEMOCRACY">democracy</a> there can be no exercise of sovereignty but by suffrage, which is the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the people's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>. In all democracies, therefore, it is of the utmost importance to regulate by whom, and in what manner, the suffrages are to be given. And the Athenians were so justly jealous of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a>, that a stranger, who interfered in the assemblies of the people, was punished by their laws with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; because such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was deemed guilty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, by usurping those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of sovereignty to which he had no <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, where the people do not debate in a collective body, but by representation, the exercise of this sovereignty consists in the choice of representatives. The laws have therefore very strictly guarded against usurpation <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> abuse of this power, by many salutary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>; which may be reduced to these three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, 1. The qualifications of the electors. 2. The qualifications of the elected. 3. The proceedings at elections. (1.) As to the qualifications of the electors. The true reason of requiring any qualification, with regard to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, in voters, is to exclude such persons as are in so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> a situation, that they are esteemed to have no will of their own. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> these persons had votes, they would be tempted to dispose of them under some undue influence or other. This would give a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, an artful, or a wealthy man, a larger share in elections than is consistent with general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. If it were probable that every man would give his vote freely, and without influence of any kind; then, upon the true <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and genuine principles of liberty, every member of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, however <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, should have a vote in electing those delegates to whose <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> is committed the disposal of his property, his liberty, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. But since that can hardly be expected in persons of indigent fortunes, or such as are under the immediate dominion of others, all popular states have been obliged to establish certain qualifications; whereby some, who are suspected to have no will of their own, are excluded from voting, in order to let other individuals, whose will may be supposed independent, more thoroughly upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with each other. And this constitution of suffrages is framed upon a wiser principle with us, than either of the methods of voting, by centuries, or by tribes, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. In the method by centuries, instituted by Servius Tullius, it was principally property, and not numbers, that turned the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>: in the method by tribes, gradually introduced by the tribunes of the people, numbers only were regarded, and property entirely overlooked. Hence the laws passed by the former method had usually too great a tendency to aggrandize the patricians or rich <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>; and those by the latter had too much of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVELLING">levelling</a> principle. Our constitution fleers between the two extremes. Only such are entirely excluded as can have no will of their own; there is hardly a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> to be found, but what is intitled to a vote in some <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> or other in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Nor is comparative wealth, or property, entirely disregarded in elections; for though the richest man has only one vote at one place, yet, if his property be at all diffused, he has probably a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to vote at more places than one, and therefore has many representatives. This is the spirit of our constitution; not that we assert it is in fact quite so perfect as we have endeavoured to describe it; for if any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> might be wished or suggested in the present form of parliaments, it should be in favour of a more complete representation of the people. But to return to the qualifications; and first those of electors for knights of the shire. 1. By statute 8 Hen. VI. c. 7, and 10 Hen. VI. c. 2. (amended by 14 Geo. III. c. 58.) the knights of the shire shall be chosen of people, whereof every man shall have freehold to the value of forty shillings by the year within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; which (by subsequent statutes) is to be clear of all charges and deductions, except parliamentary and parochial taxes. The knights of shires are the representatives of the landholders, or landed <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the kingdom: their electors must therefore have estates in lands or tenements within the county represented. Election. fented. These estates must be freehold, that is, for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of life at least; because beneficial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEASES">leases</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> terms of years were not in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> at the making of these statutes, and copyholders were then little better than villains, absolutely dependent upon their lords. This freehold must be of 40 shillings annual value; because that sum would then, with proper industry, furnish all the necessaries of life, and render the freeholder, if he pleased, an independent man: For Bishop Fleetwood, in his Chronicon Precisum, written at the beginning of the last century, has fully proved 40 shillings in the reign of Henry VI. to have been equal to 12 pounds per annum in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>; and, as the value of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is very considerably lowered since the bishop wrote, we may fairly conclude, from this and other circumstances, that what was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to 12 pounds in his days, is equivalent to 20 at present. The other less important qualifications of the electors for counties in England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> may be collected from the statutes cited below (a); which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, 1. That no person under 21 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> shall be capable of voting for any member. This extends to all sorts of members as well for boroughs as counties; as does also the next, viz. 3. That no person convicted of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">perjury</a>, or subornation of perjury, shall be capable of voting in any election. 4. That no person shall vote in right of any freehold, granted to him fraudulently, to qualify him to vote. Fraudulent grants are such as contain an agreement to re-convey, or to defeat the estate granted; which agreements are made void, and the estate is absolutely vested in the person to whom it is so granted. And, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the better against such frauds, it is further provided, 5. That every voter shall have been in the actual possession, or receipt of the profits, of his freehold to his own use for 12 <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> months before; except it came to him by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, marriage settlement, will, or promotion to a benefice or office. 6. That no person shall vote in respect of an annuity or rent-charge, unless registered with the clerk of the peace 12 calendar months before. 7. That in mortgaged or trust estates, the person in possession, under the above-mentioned restrictions, shall have the vote. 8. That only one person shall be admitted to vote for any one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or tenement, to prevent the splitting of freeholds. 9. That no estate shall qualify a voter, unless the estate has been affected to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>-tax aid, at least 12 months before the election. 10. That no tenant by copy of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>-roll shall be permitted to vote as a freeholder. Thus much for the electors in counties. As for the electors of citizens and burgesses, these are supposed to be the mercantile part or trading interest of this kingdom. But as trade is of a fluctuating <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and seldom long fixed in a place, it was formerly left to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> to summon, pro re nata, the most flourishing <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> to send representatives to parliament. So that as towns increased in trade, and grew populous, they were admitted to a share in the legislature. But the misfortune is, that the deserted boroughs <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be summoned, as well as those to whom their trade and inhabitants were transferred; except a few which petitioned to be eased of the expense, then usual, of maintaining their members: four shillings a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> being allowed for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> of the shire, and two shillings for a citizen or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a>; which was the rate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> established in the reign of Edward III. Hence the members for boroughs now bear above a quadruple proportion to those for counties; and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of parliament men is increased since Fortescue's times, in the reign of Henry VI. from 300 to upwards of 500, exclusive of those for Scotland. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a> were, in general, not empowered to send burgesses to parliament; though once, in 28 Edw. I. when a parliament was summoned to consider of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s right to Scotland, there were issued writs, which required the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> to send up four or five, and that of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> two or three, of their most discreet and learned lawyers for that purpose. But it was King James I. who indulged them with the permanent privilege to send constantly two of their own body; to serve for those students who, though useful members of the community, were neither concerned in the landed nor the trading interest; and to protect in the legislature the rights of the republic of letters. The right of election in boroughs is various, depending entirely on the several charters, customs, and constitutions of the respective places; which has occasioned infinite dilutes; though now, by statute 2 Geo. II. c. 24, the right of voting for the future shall be allowed according to the last determination of the house of commons concerning it; and, by statute 3 Geo. III. c. 15, no freeman of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> or borough (other than such as claim by birth, marriage, or servitude) shall be entitled to vote therein, unless he hath been admitted to his freedom 12 calendar months before. (2.) Next, as to the qualifications of persons to be elected members of the house of commons. Some of these depend upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of parliaments, declared by the house of commons; others upon certain statutes. And from these it appears, 1. That they must not be aliens born or minors. 2. That they must not be any of the 12 judges, because they fit in the lords' house; nor of the clergy, for they fit in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVOCATION">convocation</a>; nor persons attainted of treason, or felony, for they are unfit to sit anywhere. 3. That sheriffs of counties, and mayors and bailiffs of boroughs, are not eligible in their respective jurisdictions, as being returning officers; but that sheriffs of one county are eligible to be knights of another. 4. That, in strictness, all members ought to have been inhabitants of the places for which they are chosen; but this, having been long disregarded, was at length entirely repealed by statute 14 Geo. III. c. 58. 5. That no persons concerned in the management of any duties or taxes created since 1692, except the commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a>, nor any of the officers following (viz. commissioners of prizes, transports, sick and wounded, wine licenses, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, and victualling; secretaries or receivers of prizes; controllers of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> accounts; agents for regiments; governors of plantations, and their (a) 7 and 8 Will. III. c. 25. 10 Ann. c. 23. 2 Geo. II. c. 21. 18 Geo. II. c. 18. 31 Geo. II. c. 14. 3 Geo. III. c. 24. Election. their deputies; officers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a> or Gibraltar; officers of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCISE">excise</a> and customs; clerks or deputies in the several offices of the treasury, exchequer, navy, victualling, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, pay of the army or navy, secretaries of state, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, stamps, appeals, wine-licenses, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HACKNEY">hackney</a>-coaches, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAWKERS">hawkers</a>, and pedlars), nor any persons that hold any new office under the crown created since 1705, are capable of being elected or fitting as members. 6. That no person having a pension under the crown during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, or for any term of years, is capable of being elected or fitting. 7. That if any member accepts an office under the crown, except an officer in the army or navy accepting a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a>, his seat is void; but such member is capable of being re-elected. 8. That all knights of the shire shall be actual knights, or such notable esquires and gentlemen as have estates sufficient to be knights, and by no means of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of yeomen. This is reduced to a still greater certainty, by ordaining, 9. That every knight of a shire shall have a clear estate of freehold or copyhold to the value of £600 per annum, and every citizen and burgess to the value of £300; except the eldest sons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> and of persons qualified to be knights of shires, and except the members for the two universities; which somewhat balances the ascendant which the boroughs have gained over the counties, by obliging the trading interest to make choice of landed men: and of this qualification the member must make oath, and give in the particulars in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his taking his seat. But, subject to these standing restrictions and disqualifications, every subject of the realm is eligible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> right: though there are instances, wherein persons in particular circumstances have forfeited that common right, and have been declared ineligible for that parliament, by a vote of the house of commons, or for ever, by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the legislature. But it was an unconstitutional prohibition, which was grounded on an ordinance of the house of lords, and inserted in the king's writs, for the parliament held at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVENTRY">Coventry</a>, 6 Hen. IV. that no apprentice or other man of the law should be elected a knight for the shire therein; in return for which, our lawbooks and historians have branded this parliament with the name of parliamentum indocilem, or the lack-learning parliament; and Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> observes with some spleen, that there was never a good law made thereat. (3.) The third point, regarding elections, is the method of proceeding therein. This is also regulated by the law of parliament, and the several statutes referred to in the margin below (b); all which we shall blend together, and extract out of them a summary account of the method of proceeding to elections. As soon as the parliament is summoned, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> (or if a vacancy happens during the sitting of parliament, the speaker, by order of the house, and without such order if a vacancy happens by death in the time of a recess for upwards of 20 days) sends his warrant to the clerk of the crown in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>; who thereupon issues out writs to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of every county, for the election of all the members to serve for that county, and every city and borough therein. Within three days after the receipt of this writ, the sheriff is to send his precept, under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>, to the proper returning officers of the cities and boroughs, commanding them to elect their members; and the said returning officers are to proceed to election within eight days from the receipt of the precept, giving four days notice of the same; and to return the persons chosen, together with the precept, to the sheriff. But elections of knights of the shire must be proceeded to by the sheriffs themselves in person, at the next county-court that shall happen after the delivery of the writ. The county court is a court held every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> or oftener by the sheriff, intended to try little causes not exceeding the value of 40s. in what part of the county he pleases to appoint for that purpose: but for the election of knights of the shire, it must be held at the most usual place. If the county-court falls upon the day of delivering the writ, or within six days after, the sheriff may adjourn the court and election to some other convenient time, not longer than 16 days, nor shorter than 10: but he cannot alter the place, without the consent of all the candidates; and, in all such <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, 10 days public notice must be given of the time and place of the election. And, as it is essential to the very being of parliament that elections should be absolutely free, therefore all undue influences upon the electors are illegal, and strongly prohibited. For Mr Locke ranks it among those breaches of trust in the executive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, which, according to his notions, amount to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, "if he employs the force, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>, and offices of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> to corrupt the representatives, or openly to pre-engage the electors, and prescribe what manner of persons shall be chosen: For thus to regulate candidates and electors, and new-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> the ways of election, what is it (says he) but to cut up the government by the roots and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> the very fountain of public security?" As soon, therefore, as the time and place of election, either in counties or boroughs, are fixed, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> quartered in the place are to remove, at least one day before the election, to the distance of two miles or more; and not to return till one day after the poll is ended. Riots likewise have been frequently determined to make an election void. By vote also of the house of commons, to whom alone belongs the power of determining contested elections, no lord of parliament, or lord-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of a county, hath any right to interfere in the election of commoners; and, by statute, the lord warden of the cinque-ports shall not recommend any members there. If any officer of the excise, customs, stamps, or certain other branches of the revenue, presume to intermeddle in elections, by persuading any voter or diffusing him, he forfeits 100l. and is disabled to hold any office. Thus (b) 7 Hen. IV. c. 15. 8 Hen. VI. c. 7. 23 Hen. VI. c. 14. 1 W. & M. st. 1. c. 2. 2 W. & M. st. 1. c. 7. 5 and 6 W. & M. c. 20. 7 W. III. c. 4. 7 and 8 W. III. c. 7. and c. 25. 10 & 11 W. III. c. 7. 12 and 13 W. III. c. 10. 6 Ann. c. 23. 9 Ann. c. 5. 10 Ann. c. 19. and c. 33. 2 Geo. II. c. 24. 8 Geo. II. c. 30. 18 Geo. II. c. 18. 19 Geo. II. c. 28. 10 Geo. III. c. 16. 11 Geo. III. c. 42. 14 Geo. III. c. 15. Thus are the electors of one branch of the legislature secured from any undue influence from either of the other two, and from all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> violence and compulsion. But the greatest danger is that in which themselves co-operate, by the infamous practice of bribery and corruption. To prevent which it is enacted, that no candidate shall, after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">date</a> (usually called the tele) of the writs, or after the vacancy, give any money or entertainment to his electors, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> to give any, either to particular persons, or to the place in general, in order to his being elected; on pain of being incapable to serve for that place in parliament. And if any money, gift, office, employment, or reward be given, or promised to be given, to any voter, at any time, in order to influence him to give or withhold his vote, as well he that takes as he that offers such bribe forfeits 500l. and is for ever disabled from voting and holding any office in any corporation; unless, before conviction, he will discover some other offender of the same kind, and then he is indemnified for his own offence. The first instance that occurs of election bribery, was so early as 13 Eliz. when one Thomas Longe (being a simple man, and of small capacity to serve in parliament) acknowledged that he had given the returning officer and others of the borough for which he was chosen four pounds to be returned member, and was for that premium elected. But for this offence the borough was amerced, the member was removed, and the officer fined and imprisoned. But as this practice hath since taken much deeper and more universal root, it hath occasioned the making of these wholesome statutes; to complete the efficacy of which, there is nothing wanting but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> and integrity to put them in strict execution. Undue influence being thus guarded against, the election is to be proceeded to on the day appointed; the sheriff or other returning officer first taking an oath against bribery, and for the due execution of his office. The candidates likewise, if required, must swear to their qualification, and the electors in counties to theirs; and the electors both in counties and boroughs are also compelled to take the oath of abjuration, and that against bribery and corruption. And it might not be amiss, if the members elected were bound to take the latter oath as well as the former; which, in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, would be much more effectual than administering it only to the electors. The election being closed, the returning officer in boroughs returns his precept to the sheriff, with the persons elected by the majority; and the sheriff returns the whole, together with the writ for the county and the knights elected thereupon, to the clerk of the crown in chancery; before the day of meeting, if it be a new parliament, or within 14 days after the election, if it be an occasional vacancy; and this under penalty of 500l. If the sheriff does not return such knights only as are duly elected, he forfeits, by the old statutes of Henry VI. 100l.; and the returning officer in boroughs, for a like false return, 40l.; and they are besides liable to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> damages shall be recovered, by the later statutes of King William: and any person bribing the returning officer shall also forfeit 300l. But the members returned by him are the fitting members, until the house of commons, upon petition, shall adjudge the return to be false and illegal. The form and manner of proceeding upon such petition are now regulated by statute 1 Geo. III. c. 16. (amended by 11 Geo. III. c. 42. and made perpetual by 14 Geo. III. c. 15.), which directs the method of choosing by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> a select committee of 15 members, who are sworn well and truly to try the same, and a true judgment to give, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. Election of Scots Peers. See Lords. Election of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> Persons. Elections for the dignities of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> ought to be free, according to the stat. 9 Ed. II. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 14. If any persons, that have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> in elections, take any reward for an election in any church, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, school, &c. the election shall be void. And if any persons of such <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> resign their places to others for reward, they incur a forfeiture of double the sum; and both the parties are rendered incapable of the place. Stat. 31 Eliz. cap. 6. Election of a Verderor of the Forest (electione viridariorum forelic), in Law, a writ that lies for the choice of a verderor, where any of the verderors of the forest are dead, or removed from their offices. This writ is directed to the sheriff, and the verderor is to be elected by the freeholders of the county, in the same manner as coroners. New Nat. Brev. 366. Election is also the state of a person who is left to his own free will, to take or do either one thing or another, which he pleases. See Liberty. Election, in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, signifies the choice which God, of his good pleasure, makes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> or men, for the objects of mercy and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>. The election of the Jews was the choice God made of that people to be more immediately attached to his worship and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and for the Messiah to be born of them. And thus particular nations were elected to the participation of the outward blessings of Christianity. Election also, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of some divines, signifies a predetermination to grace and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>, and sometimes to glory only. And it has been enjoined as an article of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, that predetermination to grace is gratuitous, merely and simply so; gratia, quia gratis <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATA">data</a>. But the divines are much divided as to the point, whether election to glory be gratuitous, or whether it supposes obedience and good works, i.e. whether it be before or after the provision of our obedience. See Grace and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REPROBATION">Reprobation</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTIVE">Elective</a>, something that is done, or passes, by election. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">Elector</a>. Some benefices are elective, others collative. Municipal offices in England are generally elective; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, venal. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> is an elective kingdom. Elective <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">Attraction</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Elector, a person who has a right to elect or choose another to an office, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, &c. See Election. Elector is particularly, and by way of eminence, applied to those princes of Germany in whom lies the right of electing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>; being all sovereign princes, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> members of the empire. The electoral college, consisting of all the electors of the empire, is the most illustrious and august body in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Bellarmine and Baronius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of it to Pope Gregory V. and the emperor O- Elector. tho III. in the tenth century; of which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> are the generality of historians, and particularly the canonists: however, the number of electors was unsettled, at least, till the 13th century. In 1356 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> IV., by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> bull, fixed the number of electors to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>; three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, viz. the archbishops of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MENTZ">Mentz</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREVES">Treves</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>; and four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a>, viz. the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOHEMIA">Bohemia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNT">count</a> Palatine of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, and marquis of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>. In 1648 this order was changed, the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a> being put in the place of the count Palatine, who having accepted the crown of Bohemia was outlawed by the emperor; but being at length restored, an eighth <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTORATE">electorate</a> was erected for the duke of Bavaria. In 1692, a ninth electorate was created, by the emperor Leopold, in favour of the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>, of the house of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUNSWICK">Brunswick</a>-Lüneburg. There is this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the secular and ecclesiastical electors, that the first have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a> voice, that is, may choose and be chosen; the last, an active only. The three archbishops are to be 30 years old before they can be advanced to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>; the seculars 18, before they can perform the office themselves. These last have each their vicars, who officiate in their absence. Besides the power of choosing an emperor, the electors have also that of capitulating with and deposing him; so that, if there be one suffrage wanting, a protest may be entered against the proceedings. By the right of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, they attribute to themselves great privileges, as making of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, coining, and taking care of the public interest and security of the states; and the emperor promises, upon oath, to receive the empire upon these conditions. The electors have precedence of all other princes of the empire, even of cardinals and kings; and are addressed under the title of electoral highnesses. Their several functions are as follow. The elector of Mentz is chancellor of Germany, convokes the states, and gives his vote before any of the rest. The elector of Cologne is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> chancellor of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and consecrates the emperor. The elector of Treves is chancellor of the Gauls, and confers imposition of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> upon the emperor. The count Palatine of the Rhine is great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the empire, and presents the emperor with a globe at his coronation. The elector of Bavaria is great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and carries the golden apple. The marquis of Brandenburg is grand-chamberlain, and puts the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> on the emperor's finger. The elector of Saxony is grand marshal, and gives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> to the emperor. The king of Bohemia is grand <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">butler</a>, and puts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>'s crown on the emperor's head. Lastly, the elector of Hanover, now king of Great Britain, is <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>-treasurer, though first erected under the title of standard-bearer of the empire.

ELECTORATE

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used as well to signify the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of, as the territories belonging to, any of the electors of Germany; such are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a>, &c. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELECTOR">ELECTOR</a>.

ELECTRIC

Pages 255-255

derived from ἐλεκτρόν, "<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>," in physics, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to those substances, in which the electric fluid is capable of being excited, and accumulated without transmitting it, and therefore called non-conductors. See <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">ELECTRICITY</a>.

ELECTRICITY

Pages 345-440

Principles of Electricity illustrated by experiment. Exper. 3.—Into a jar, coated on the outside, he put a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of powdered glass, and having furnished it in other respects like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> phial, he proceeded to examine whether it would receive a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>. He found that it could be completely <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the powdered glass acted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a conductor. By similar experiments M. Van Swinden found that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of sulphur acted as a conductor though more imperfectly than powdered glass. Soon after the discovery of the Leyden phial and shock produced by it, it became a desirable object with electricians to ascertain how far the shock might be conveyed, and how <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> would be required to convey it to any considerable distance. The French philosophers were the first to appear in this field, but they did little more than excite the English to go far beyond them in these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> undertakings. A circuit was made by the former of 900 toises, consisting of men holding <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wires betwixt each two, through which the electric shock was sensibly felt. At another time they made the shock <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through a wire two thousand toises in length, that is, near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> about two English miles and a half; though part of the wires dragged upon wet grass, went over chasms, hedges, or palisades and over ground newly ploughed up. Into another chain they took the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of the basin in the Tuileries, the surface of which was about an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, and the phial was discharged through it. Mr Monnier the younger, endeavoured to determine the velocity of the electric power; and for this purpose made the shock pass through an iron wire of 950 toises in length, but he could not observe that it spent a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in passing it. He also found, that when a wire of 1319 feet, with its extremities brought near together, was electrified, that the electricity ceased at one end the moment it was taken off at the other. But all these attempts of the French would scarcely have deserved to be mentioned, but that they preceded the greater, the more numerous, and more accurate experiments of the English. The names of the English gentlemen, animated with a truly philosophical spirit, and who were indefatigable in this business, deserve to be transmitted to posterity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> was Dr Watson. He planned and directed all the operations, and never failed to be present at every experiment. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> assistants were Martin Folkes, Esq., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Cavendish, Dr Bevis, Mr Graham, Dr Birch, Mr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> Daval, Mr Trembley, Mr Elliot, Mr Robins, and Mr Short. Many other persons, and some of distinction, gave their attendance occasionally. Dr Watson, who wrote the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of their proceedings, in order to lay them before the Royal Society, begins by observing (what was verified in all their experiments) that the electric shock is not, strictly speaking, conducted in the shortest manner possible, unless the bodies through which it passes, conduct equally well; for that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they conduct unequally, the circuit is always formed through the best conductors, though the length of it be ever so great. The first attempt these gentlemen made, was to convey the electric shock across the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, making <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the water of the river for one part of the chain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a>. This they accomplished on the 14th and 18th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> of 1747, by fastening a wire all along Westminster <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, at a considerable height above the water. One end of this wire communicated with the coating of a charged phial, the other being held by an observer, who in his other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> held an iron rod, which he dipped into the river. On the opposite side of the river stood a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who likewise dipped an iron rod in the river with one hand, and in the other held a wire, the extremity of which might be brought into contact with the wire of the phial. Upon making the discharge, the shock was felt by the observers on both sides of the river, but more sensibly by those who were stationed on the same side with the machine; part of the electric fire having gone from the wire <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the moist <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of the bridge, thereby making several shorter circuits to the phial, but still all passing through the gentlemen who were stationed on the same side with the machine. This was, in a manner demonstrated by some persons feeling a sensible shock in their arms and feet, who only happened to touch the wire at the time of one of the discharges, when they were standing upon wet steps which led to the river. Upon this and the subsequent occasions, the gentlemen made use of wires, in preference to chains, for this reason among other reasons, that the electricity which was conducted by chains, was not so strong as that conducted by wires. This, as they well observed, was occasioned by the junctures of the links not being sufficiently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, as appeared by the flashing and snapping at every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNCTURE">juncture</a>, where there was the least separation. These lesser snappings being numerous in the whole length of a chain, very sensibly lessened the great discharge at the prime conductor. Their next attempt was to force the electrical shock to make a circuit of two miles, at the New-river at Stoke Newington. This they performed on the 24th of July 1747, at two places; at one of which, the distance by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> was 800 feet, and by water 2000; in the other the distance by land was 2800 feet, and by water 8000. The disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> was similar to what they before used at Westminster bridge, and the effect answered their utmost expectations. But, as in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, the observers at both extremities of the chain, which terminated in the water, felt the shock, as well when they stood with their rods fixed into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> 20 feet from the water, as when they were put into the river; it occasioned a doubt, whether the shock was formed through the windings of the river, or a much shorter way by the ground of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>; for the experiment plainly showed, that the meadow ground, with the grass on it, conducted the electricity very well. By subsequent experiments, they were fully convinced, that the electricity had not in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> been conveyed by the water of the river, which was two miles in length, but by land, where the distance was only one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a>; in which space, however, the electric power must necessarily have passed over the New-river twice, have gone through several gravel pits, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stubble field. † p. 360. On the 28th of July they repeated the experiment at the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, with the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of circumstances. The iron wire was, in its whole length, supported by dry sticks, and the observers stood upon original electrics; the effect of which was, that they felt the shock much more sensibly than when the conducting wire had lain upon the ground, and when the observers had stood likewise upon the ground, as in the former experiment. Afterwards, everything remaining as before, the observers were directed, instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> their rods into the water, to put them into the ground, each 150 feet from the water. They were both smartly struck, though they were distant from each other above 500 feet. The same gentlemen, pleased with the success of their former experiments, undertook another, the object of which was to determine, whether the electric power could be conveyed through dry ground; and at the same time to carry it through water to a greater distance than they had done before. For this purpose they pitched upon Highbury-barn, beyond Illington, where they carried it into execution on the 5th of August 1747. They chose a station for their machine almost equally distant from two other stations for observers, upon the New-river, which were somewhat more than a mile asunder by land, and two miles by water. They had found the streets of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, when dry, to conduct very strongly, for about 40 yards; and the dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> at Newington about the same distance. The event of this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> answered their expectations. The electric fire made the circuit of the water when both the wires and the observers were supported on original electrics, and the rods dipped into the river. They also both felt the shock, when one of the observers was placed in a dry gravelly pit, about 300 yards nearer the machine than the former station, and 100 yards distant from the river; from which the gentlemen were satisfied, that the dry gravelly ground had conducted the electricity as strongly as water. The last attempt of this kind which these gentlemen made, and which required all their sagacity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> in the conduct of it, was to try whether the electric shock was perceptible at twice the distance to which they had before carried it, in ground perfectly dry, and where no water was near, and also to distinguish, if possible, the comparative velocity of electricity, and of found. For this purpose they fixed upon Shooter's-hill, and made their first experiment on the 14th of August 1747, a time, when, as it happened, but one shower of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> had fallen during five preceding weeks. The wire communicating with the iron rod, which made the discharge, was 6732 feet in length, and was supported all the way upon baked sticks; as was also the wire which communicated with the coating of the phial, which was 3868 feet long, and the observers were distant from each other two miles. The result of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> demonstrated, to the satisfaction of the gentlemen present, that the circuit performed by the electricity was four miles, viz., two miles of wire, and two of dry ground, the space between the extremities of the wires, a distance, which, without trial, as they justly observed, was too great to be credited. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> was discharged at the instant of the explosion, and the observers had stop watches in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> the moment when they felt the shock; but as far as they could distinguish, the time in which the electric power performed that vast circuit was instantaneous. In all the explosions where the circuit was made of any considerable length, it was observed, that though the phial was very well charged, yet that the snap at the gun-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> made by the explosion was not near so loud as when the circuit was formed in a room; so that a bystander, says Dr Watson, would not imagine, from seeing the flash and hearing the report, that the stroke, at the extremity of the conducting wire, would have been considerable, the contrary of which, when the wires were properly managed, he says, always happened. Still the gentlemen, unrestrained in these pursuits, were desirous of ascertaining, if possible, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> velocity of electricity though a certain space; because, though in the last experiment, the time of its progress was certainly very small, they were desirous of knowing, small as that time might be, whether it was measurable, and Dr Watson had contrived an excellent method for that purpose. Accordingly, on the 5th of August 1748, the gentlemen met for the last time, at Shooter's-hill; when it was agreed to make an electric circuit of two miles, by several turnings of the wire, in the same field. The middle of this circuit they contrived to be in the same room with the machine, where an observer took in each hand one of the extremities of the wires, each of which was a mile in length. In this excellent disposition of the apparatus, in which the time between the explosion and the shock could be observed with the greatest exactness, the phial was discharged several times; but the observer always felt himself shocked at the very instant of making the explosion. Upon this the gentlemen were fully satisfied, that through the whole length of this wire, which was 12,276 feet in length, the velocity of the electric power was instantaneous. We have noticed the increased <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> from liquids by means of electricity. The following experiment, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> exhibited by lecturers on electricity, is usually considered of the same kind. Stick a small piece of sealing-wax on the end of a wire, and set fire to it. Then put an electrical machine in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and present the wax <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> blown out at the distance of some inches from the prime conductor. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of extremely fine filaments <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> immediately dart from the sealing wax to the conductor, on which they will be condensed into a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, resembling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. If the wire with the sealing-wax be stuck into one of the holes of the conductor, and a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> be presented at a moderate distance to the wax, just after it has been ignited, on setting the machine in motion, a network of wax will be formed on the paper. The same effect, but in a slighter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, will be produced, if the paper be briskly rubbed with a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a>, and the melting sealing-wax be held pretty near the paper immediately after rubbing. If the paper thus painted, as it were, with sealing-wax, be gently warmed by holding the back of it to the fire, the wax will adhere to it, and the result of the experiment will thus be rendered permanent. A beautiful experiment of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> is made Electricity illustrated by experiment. To make camphor flow into ramifications. Curious experiment of Professor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LICHTENBERG">Lichtenberg</a>. The electrophorus, that is, a plate of some resinous substance, as sulphur, rosin, gum-lac, &c., is first excited, either by rubbing or otherwise; then a piece of metal of any shape, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, as for instance, a three-legged compass, a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> tube, or the like, is set upon the electrophorus, and to this piece of metal, so placed, a spark is given, of the electricity contrary to that of the plate; this done, the piece of metal is removed, by means of a stick of sealing-wax or other electric, and some powder of rosin, kept in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> bag, is shaken upon the electrophorus; this powder will be found to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> about those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> upon the plate, which the piece of metal touched, forming some radiated appearances, much like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> representations of flares; at the same time, upon the greatest part of the plate, that is, besides those flares, there is hardly any powder at all. Now, it is to be remarked, that if the plate be excited negatively, and the spark given to the metal set upon it is positive, the appearance will be as above described; but if, on the contrary, the plate is positive and the spark is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, then the powder of rosin will be found to fall upon those parts of the plate which in the other case is left uncovered, and to leave the flares clean; in short, it will do just the reverse of what it did in the other case; or, in other words, the powder of rosin will be attracted by those parts only of the electrophorus which are electrified positively. The configurations produced in the above experiment of M. Lichtenberg appeared to curious that they were soon imitated by various electricians, particularly by Mr Cavallo and the Reverend <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> Benney, inventor of the doubler. The directions given by this last gentleman are as follows. To make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> figures, take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of rasped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a> wood; put it into a kettle with as much water as will cover it, or rather more; also put in about an ounce of gum arabic and a lump of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a> about as big as a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>; let it boil about two hours, or till the water is strongly coloured; strain off the extract into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISH">dish</a>, and set it in an iron oven, where it is to remain till all the water be evaporated, which with me was effected in about twelve hours; but this depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the oven, which should not be so hot as to endanger its <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. Sometimes I have boiled the strained extract till it was considerably infusified before it was placed in the oven, that it might be sooner dry. When it is quite dry but not burnt, scrape it out of the dish, and grind it in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> till it be finely pulverized. In doing this, it is proper to cover the mortar with a cloth, having a hole through to prevent the powder from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> away and offending the nose, and also to do it out of doors if the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> be dry and calm, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> may carry away the powder necessarily escaping, and which otherwise is very disagreeable. When ground fine, let it be sifted through muslin or a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>-sieve, returning the coarser part into the mortar to be ground again. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> and sifting are finished, the powder is ready for use. The resinous plate I have mostly used was composed of five pounds of rosin, half a pound of bees-wax, and two ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, melted together, and poured upon a board fifteen inches <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, with ribs upon the edges at least half an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, to confine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> whilst fluid; thus the resinous plate was half an inch thick, which is better than a thinner plate, the figures being more distinct. After the composition is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, it will be found covered with small blisters, which may be taken out by holding the plate before the fire, till the surface be melted, then let it cool again, and upon holding it a second time to the fire, more blisters will appear; but by thus repeatedly heating and cooling the surface, it will at last become perfectly smooth. Some plates were made smaller, and the resinous composition confined to the form of an ellipse, a circle, or escutcheon, by a rim of tin half an inch broad, and fixed upon a board. The next thing to be done is to prepare the paper, which is to be softened in water, either by laying the pieces upon each other in a vessel of cold water, or first pouring a little hot water upon the bottom of a large dish, then laying upon it a piece of paper, so that one edge of the paper may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> over the edge of the dish, to remain dry; that it may afterwards be more conveniently taken up. Then pour more hot water upon its upper surface. Upon this place another piece in the same manner, again pouring on more water, and thus proceed till all the pieces are laid in. By using hot water, the paper will be more softened in a few minutes than if it remains in cold water a whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. When the figures are to be made, the resinous plate must lie horizontally, whilst the electricity is communicated, if the experiment requires anything to be placed upon the plate; but it is convenient afterwards to hang it up in a vertical position whilst the powder is projected, lest too much powder should fall where it is not required. A little of the powder may be taken between a finger and thumb, and projected by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> it over a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>; or, which is better, a quantity of powder may be put into the bellows and blown towards the plate. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is sufficiently covered with powder, let the plate be again laid horizontally upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; then take one of the softened papers out of the water by its dry edge, and lay it carefully between the leaves of a book, pressing the book together, and let it lie in this situation about half a minute. Then remove the paper to a dry place in the book, and press it again about the same time, which will generally be sufficient to take off the superfluous moisture. Then take up the paper by the two corners of its dry edge, and place the wet edge a little beyond the figure on the resinous plate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOWERING">lowering</a> the rest of the piece gradually till it covers the figure without sliding; then lay over it a piece of clean dry paper, and press it gently; let it remain a short time, and then rub it closer to the plate with a cloth, or, which is better, press it down by means of a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a> covered with cloth, taking care that the paper be not moved from its first position. When the paper is sufficiently pressed, let it be taken up by its dry Principles of dry edge, and laid upon the surface of a vessel of water Electricity with the printed side downwards; by this means the illustrated superfluous powder will sink in the water, and the by experiment figure will not be so liable afterwards to spread in the paper. After the paper has remained on the water during a few minutes, take it up and place it between the leaves of a book, removing it frequently to a dry place. If it be desired that the paper should be speedily dry, let the book-leaves in which it is to be placed be previously warmed, and by removing it to several places it will be dry much sooner than by holding it near a fire, and without drawing the paper crooked. By the above <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>, it is obvious, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, calico, or linen, as well as paper, may be printed with these figures, and the effects of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of electricity upon a refrinous plate be exhibited to those who have not leisure or inclination to perform the experiments. The figures represented in Plate CXCII. were formed much after Mr Bennet's method. The apparatus used for making them consisted only of a common Leyden phial, and a plate of glass 15 inches square, covered on one side with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> of gum-lac dissolved in spirit of wine, and several times laid over. The other side is covered with tin-foil laid on with common paste. When it is to be used, the glass plate is put upon a metallic stand, with the tin-foil side laid undermost; the phial is to be charged, and the knob drawn over the varnished side. Thus any kind of figure may be drawn, or letters made, as represented in the plate; and from every figure beautiful ramifications will proceed, longer or shorter according to the strength of the charge. On some occasions, however, the charge may be too strong, particularly where we wish to represent letters, so that the whole will be blended into one confused <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. The round figures are formed by placing metallic rings or plates upon the electrical plate; and then giving them a spark from the electrified bottle, or sending a shock through them. The figures may be rendered permanent by blowing off the loose chalk, and clapping on a piece of black-sized paper upon them; or if they are wanted of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, they may easily be obtained by means of lake, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERMILION">vermilion</a>, rose-pink, or any of the ordinary colours ground very fine. The easiest way of applying them seems to be by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARBER">barber</a>'s puff bellows. We shall conclude this part of our article with noticing the effects produced by electricity on magnetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>. These may be stated in the following proposition. An electric shock communicates a magnetic power to needles, and frequently reverses or destroys that polarity. By electricity Dr Franklin frequently gave polarity to needles and reversed them at pleasure. A shock from four large jars, sent through a fine sewing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, he says, gave it polarity, so that it would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> when laid on water. What is most remarkable in these electrical experiments upon magnets is, that if the needle, when it was struck, lay east and west, the end which was entered by the electric blast pointed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>; but that if it lay north and south, the end which lay to wards the north would continue to point north, whether the fire entered at that end or the contrary; though he imagined that a stronger stroke would have reversed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> even in that situation, an effect which had been known to have been produced by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>. He also observed, that the polarity was strongest when the needle was struck lying north and south, and weakest when it lay east and west. He takes notice that, in these experiments the needle, in some cases, would be finely blued like the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of a watch, by the electric <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>; in which case, the colour given by a flash from two jars only might be wiped off, but that a flash from four jars fixed it, and frequently melted the needles. The jars which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> used held <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight gallons, and were coated and lined with tin-foil. Dr Van Marum made several experiments on communicating polarity to needles with his very powerful machine. He and his coadjutor tried to give polarity to needles made of watch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> from three to five inches in length, and likewise to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> bars <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches long, from a quarter of an inch to half an inch broad, and about a line in thickness. The result was, that when the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> or needle was placed horizontally in the magnetic meridian, whichever way the shock entered, the end of the bar that stood toward the north acquired the north polarity, or the power of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> towards the north when freely suspended, and the opposite end acquired the south. If the bar, before it received the shock, had some polarity, and was placed with its poles contrary to the usual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, then its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> polarity was always diminished, and often reversed; so that the extremity of it, which in receiving the shock looked towards the north, became the north pole, &c. When the bar or needle was struck standing perpendicularly, its lowest end became the north pole in any case, even when the bar had some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNETISM">magnetism</a> before, and was placed with the south pole downwards. Ceteris paribus, the bars seemed to acquire an equal degree of magnetic power, whether they were struck whilst standing horizontally in the magnetic meridian, or perpendicular to the horizon.
